From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Retail establishment

For other uses, see [Department store (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store_(disambiguation) "Department store (disambiguation)").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Bon_March%C3%A9%2C_Paris_-_interior_view.JPG/250px-Bon_March%C3%A9%2C_Paris_-_interior_view.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bon_March%C3%A9,_Paris_-_interior_view.JPG)

Interior of [Le Bon Marché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Bon_March%C3%A9 "Le Bon Marché") in Paris (2008)

A **department store** is a [retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail "Retail") establishment offering a wide range of [consumer goods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_good "Final good") in different areas of the store under one roof, each area ("department") specializing in a product category. In modern major cities, department stores emerged in the mid-19th century, reshaping shopping habits and the definition of service and luxury. Similar developments were under way in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") (with [Whiteleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiteleys "Whiteleys")), in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") ([Le Bon Marché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Bon_March%C3%A9 "Le Bon Marché")) and in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") ([Stewart's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Turney_Stewart "Alexander Turney Stewart")).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-1)

Today, departments often include the following: clothing, cosmetics, [do it yourself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_it_yourself "Do it yourself"), [furniture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furniture "Furniture"), gardening, hardware, [home appliances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_appliance "Home appliance"), [houseware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household_goods "Household goods"), paint, sporting goods, toiletries, and toys. Additionally, other lines of products such as food, books, jewellery, electronics, [stationery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationery "Stationery"), [photographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photography "Photography") equipment, baby products, and products for pets are sometimes included. Customers generally check out near the front of the store in [discount department stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discount_store "Discount store"), while high-end traditional department stores include sales counters within each department. Some stores are one of many within a larger [retail chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_chain "Retail chain"), while others are independent retailers.

Since the 1980s, department stores have faced increasing competition from discount retailers, and later from [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce") businesses in the 2000s.

## Types

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Types")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Kuopion_Sokos2_-_Haapaniemenkatu_24-26_-_Multim%C3%A4ki_-_Kuopio_-_m.jpg/250px-Kuopion_Sokos2_-_Haapaniemenkatu_24-26_-_Multim%C3%A4ki_-_Kuopio_-_m.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kuopion_Sokos2_-_Haapaniemenkatu_24-26_-_Multim%C3%A4ki_-_Kuopio_-_m.jpg)

[Sokos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sokos "Sokos") department store building in [Multimäki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multim%C3%A4ki "Multimäki"), [Kuopio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuopio "Kuopio"), Finland

Department stores can be classified in several ways:

*   **Mainline department store** or simply, the traditional department store, offering mid- to high-end goods, most or at least some of the time at the full retail price. Examples are [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's"), [Bloomingdale's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomingdale's "Bloomingdale's"), [Nordstrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordstrom "Nordstrom"), [J.C. Penney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J.C._Penney "J.C. Penney"), [Montgomery Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_Ward "Montgomery Ward"), [Sears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears "Sears") and [Belk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belk "Belk").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-2)
    *   **[Junior department store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_department_store "Junior department store")**, a term used principally in the second part of the 20th century for a smaller version of a mainline department store. These were usually either independent stores, or chains such as [Boston Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Store_(California) "Boston Store (California)") and [Harris & Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_&_Frank "Harris & Frank"), which specialized in cosmetics and wearing apparel and accessories, with few home goods.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-4)

*   **Discount department store**, a large [discount store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discount_store "Discount store") selling apparel and home furnishings at a discount, either selling overstock from mainline department stores, or merchandise especially made for the discount department store market. Examples are [Nordstrom Rack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordstrom_Rack "Nordstrom Rack"), [Saks Off 5th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saks_Off_5th "Saks Off 5th"), [Marshalls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshalls "Marshalls"), [Ross Dress for Less](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Dress_for_Less "Ross Dress for Less"), [TJ Maxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TJ_Maxx "TJ Maxx"), and [Kohl's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kohl's "Kohl's").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-mainline-5)

Some sources may refer to the following types of stores as department stores, even though they are not generally considered as such:

*   [Hypermarkets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypermarket "Hypermarket") (discount superstores with full grocery offerings, such as [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation "Target Corporation"), [Walmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmart "Walmart") and [Carrefour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrefour "Carrefour"))[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-6)
*   [Variety stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_store "Variety store"), also known in the U.S. as [five and dimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_and_dime "Five and dime"), or dollar stores

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

### Origins in England, 1700s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Origins in England, 1700s")]

One of the first department stores may have been Bennett's in [Derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby "Derby"), first established as an [ironmonger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironmonger "Ironmonger") (hardware shop) in 1734.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-Bennetts-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-derbyshire-8) It continued trading in the same building until its administration and closure in 2019.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-Bennetts-7) However, the first reliably dated department store to be established, was [Harding, Howell & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harding,_Howell_&_Co. "Harding, Howell & Co."), which opened in 1796 on [Pall Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pall_Mall,_London "Pall Mall, London"), London.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-9) The oldest department store chain may be [Debenhams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debenhams "Debenhams"), which was established in 1778 and closed in 2021. It is the longest trading defunct British retailer. An observer writing in _[Ackermann's Repository](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ackermann's\_Repository "Ackermann's Repository")_, a British periodical on contemporary taste and fashion, described the enterprise in 1809 as follows:

> The house is one hundred and fifty feet in length from front to back, and of proportionate width. It is fitted up with great taste, and is divided by glazed partitions into four departments, for the various branches of the extensive business, which is there carried on. Immediately at the entrance is the first department, which is exclusively appropriated to the sale of furs and fans. The second contains articles of haberdashery of every description, silks, muslins, lace, gloves, &etc. In the third shop, on the right, you meet with a rich assortment of jewelry, ornamental articles in ormolu, French clocks, &etc.; and on the left, with all the different kinds of perfumery necessary for the toilette. The fourth is set apart for millinery and dresses; so that there is no article of female attire or decoration, but what may be here procured in the first style of elegance and fashion. This concern has been conducted for the last twelve years by the present proprietors who have spared neither trouble nor expense to ensure the establishment of a superiority over every other in Europe, and to render it perfectly unique in its kind.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-10)

This venture is described as having all of the basic characteristics of the department store; it was a public retail establishment offering a wide range of [consumer goods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_good "Consumer good") in different departments. Jonathan Glancey for the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") writes:

> Harding, Howell & Co was focused on the needs and desires of fashionable women. Here, at last women were free to browse and shop, safely and decorously, away from home and from the company of men. These, for the main part, were newly affluent middle-class women, their good fortune – and the department store itself – nurtured and shaped by the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"). This was transforming life in London and the length and breadth of Britain at a dizzying pace on the back of energetic free trade, fecund invention, steam and sail, and a seemingly inexhaustible supply of expendable cheap labour.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-11)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Harrod%27s_%2850718173793%29.jpg/250px-Harrod%27s_%2850718173793%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harrod's_(50718173793).jpg)

[Harrods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrods "Harrods") illuminated exterior at night in Knightsbridge, London

This pioneering shop was closed down in 1820 when the [business partnership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_partnership "Business partnership") was dissolved. By the mid-to-late nineteenth century, most major [High Streets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Street "High Street") in British cities featured flourishing department stores. Increasingly, women became the main customers.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-12)[Kendals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendals "Kendals") (formerly Kendal Milne & Faulkner) in Manchester lays claim to being one of the first department stores and is still known to many of its customers as Kendal's, despite its 2005 name change to [House of Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Fraser "House of Fraser"). The Manchester institution dates back to 1836 but had been trading as Watts Bazaar since 1796.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-PB80-13) At its zenith the store had buildings on both sides of Deansgate linked by a subterranean passage "Kendals Arcade" and an art nouveau tiled food hall. The store was especially known for its emphasis on quality and style over low prices giving it the nickname "the Harrods of the North", although this was due in part to Harrods acquiring the store in 1919. [Harrods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrods "Harrods") of London can be traced back to 1834, though the current store was built between 1894 and 1905. Opened in 1830, [Austins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austins_(department_store) "Austins (department store)") in Derry remained in operation as the world's oldest independent department store until its closure in 2016.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-15)[Lewis's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis's "Lewis's") of Liverpool operated from 1856 to 2010. A concept devised by retail entrepreneur [David Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lewis_(English_merchant) "David Lewis (English merchant)"), the world's first [Christmas grotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa's_workshop "Santa's workshop") opened in Lewis's in 1879, entitled 'Christmas Fairyland'.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-16)[Liberty & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_(department_store) "Liberty (department store)") in London's [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_of_London "West End of London") gained popularity in the 1870s for selling Oriental goods.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-17) In 1889, [Oscar Wilde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Wilde "Oscar Wilde") wrote "Liberty's is the chosen resort of the artistic shopper".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-18)

### Origins in Parisian _magasins de nouveautés_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Origins in Parisian magasins de nouveautés")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Au_Bon_March%C3%A9_%28vue_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_-_gravure%29.jpg/250px-Au_Bon_March%C3%A9_%28vue_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_-_gravure%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Au_Bon_March%C3%A9_(vue_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_-_gravure).jpg)

Au Bon Marché

The Paris department stores have roots in the _magasin de nouveautés_, or [novelty stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_store?action=edit&redlink=1 "Novelty store (page does not exist)"); the first, the Tapis Rouge, was created in 1784.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-19) They flourished in the early 19th century. [Balzac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balzac "Balzac") described their functioning in his novel _[César Birotteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar\_Birotteau "César Birotteau")_. In the 1840s, with the arrival of the railroads in Paris and the increased number of shoppers they brought, they grew, and began to have large plate glass display windows, fixed prices and price tags, and advertising in newspapers.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-Fierro_(1996),_pages_911%E2%80%93912-20)

A novelty shop called _[Au Bon Marché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_Bon\_March%C3%A9 "Le Bon Marché")_ was founded in Paris in 1838 to sell items like lace, ribbons, sheets, mattresses, buttons, and umbrellas. It grew from 300 m 2 (3,200 ft 2) and 12 employees in 1838 to 50,000 m 2 (540,000 ft 2) and 1,788 employees in 1879. Boucicaut was renowned for his marketing innovations; a reading room for husbands while their wives shopped; extensive newspaper advertising; entertainment for children; and six million catalogues sent out to customers. By 1880 half the employees were women; unmarried women employees lived in dormitories on the upper floors.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-world-21)

_Au Bon Marché_ soon had [Printemps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printemps "Printemps"), founded in 1865; [La Samaritaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Samaritaine "La Samaritaine") (1869), Bazar de Hotel de Ville ([BHV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bazar_de_l'H%C3%B4tel_de_Ville "Bazar de l'Hôtel de Ville")); and [Galeries Lafayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galeries_Lafayette "Galeries Lafayette") (1895) as competitors.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-Fierro_(1996),_pages_911%E2%80%93912-20)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-22) The French gloried the national prestige brought by the Parisian stores.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-Heidrun_Homburg_1992_pp_183-219-23)[Émile Zola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Zola "Émile Zola") (1840–1902) set his novel _[Au Bonheur des Dames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au\_Bonheur\_des\_Dames "Au Bonheur des Dames")_ (1882–83) in the typical department store, making it a symbol of the new technology that was improving society and devouring it.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-24)

### First Australian department stores

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: First Australian department stores")]

Australia is notable for having the longest continuously operating department store, [David Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Jones_(department_store) "David Jones (department store)").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-:0-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-26) The first David Jones department store was opened on 24 May 1838, by Welsh born immigrant David Jones in a "large and commodious premises" on the corner of [George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Street,_Sydney "George Street, Sydney") and [Barrack Streets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrack_Street "Barrack Street") in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), only 50 years after the foundation of the colony. Expanding to a number of stores in the various states of Australia, David Jones is the oldest continuously operating department franchise in the world.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-:0-25) Other department stores in Australia include [Grace Bros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Bros "Grace Bros") founded in 1885, now merged with [Myer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myer "Myer") which was founded in 1900.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-27)

### First American department stores (1825–1858)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: First American department stores (1825–1858)")]

[Arnold Constable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Constable_&_Company "Arnold Constable & Company") was the first American department store. It was founded in 1825 as a small dry goods store on Pine Street in New York City. In 1857 the store moved into a five-story white marble dry goods palace known as the Marble House. During the Civil War, Arnold Constable was one of the first stores to issue charge bills of credit to its customers each month instead of on a bi-annual basis. The store soon outgrew the Marble House and erected a cast-iron building on Broadway and Nineteenth Street in 1869; this "Palace of Trade" expanded over the years until it was necessary to move into a larger space in 1914. Financial problems led to bankruptcy in 1975.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-28)

In New York City in 1846, [Alexander Turney Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Turney_Stewart "Alexander Turney Stewart") established the "[Marble Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/280_Broadway "280 Broadway")" on [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(Manhattan) "Broadway (Manhattan)"), between Chambers and Reade streets. He offered European retail merchandise at fixed prices on a variety of dry goods, and advertised a policy of providing "free entrance" to all potential customers. Though it was clad in white marble to look like a [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance")[palazzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo "Palazzo"), the building's [cast iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cast_iron "Cast iron") construction permitted large [plate glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_glass "Plate glass") windows that permitted major seasonal displays, especially in the Christmas shopping season. In 1862, Stewart built a new store on a full city block uptown between 9th and 10th streets, with eight floors. His innovations included buying from manufacturers for cash and in large quantities, keeping his markup small and prices low, truthful presentation of merchandise, the one-price policy (so there was no haggling), simple merchandise returns and cash refund policy, selling for cash and not credit, buyers who searched worldwide for quality merchandise, departmentalization, vertical and horizontal integration, volume sales, and free services for customers such as waiting rooms and free delivery of purchases.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-29) In 1858, [Rowland Hussey Macy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowland_Hussey_Macy "Rowland Hussey Macy") founded [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's") as a dry goods store.

### Innovations 1850–1917

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Innovations 1850–1917")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Marshall_field_interior.jpg/250px-Marshall_field_interior.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marshall_field_interior.jpg)

Marshall Field's State Street store "great hall" interior around 1910

[Marshall Field & Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Field's "Marshall Field's") originated in 1852. It was the premier department store on the busiest shopping street in the Midwest at the time, [State Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Street_(Chicago) "State Street (Chicago)") in Chicago.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-30) Marshall Field's was often cited as a model for other department stores in that it had exceptional customer service.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Marshall Field's also had the firsts; among many innovations by Marshall Field's were the first European buying office, which was located in Manchester, England, and the first bridal registry. The company was the first to introduce the concept of the personal shopper, and that service was provided without charge in every Field's store, until the chain's last days under the Marshall Field's name. It was the first store to offer revolving credit and the first department store to use [escalators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escalator "Escalator").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Marshall Field's book department in the State Street store was legendary;[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] it pioneered the concept of the "book signing". Moreover, every year at Christmas, Marshall Field's downtown store windows were filled with animated displays as part of the downtown shopping district display; the "theme" window displays became famous for their ingenuity and beauty, and visiting the Marshall Field's windows at Christmas became a tradition for Chicagoans and visitors alike, as popular a local practice as visiting the Walnut Room with its equally famous Christmas tree or meeting "under the clock" on State Street.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-31)

In 1877, [John Wanamaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wanamaker "John Wanamaker") opened what some claim was the United States' first "modern" department store in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"): the first to offer fixed prices marked on every article and also introduced electrical illumination (1878), the telephone (1879), and the use of pneumatic tubes to transport cash and documents (1880) to the department store business.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-32)

[Selfridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selfridges "Selfridges") in [Oxford Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Street "Oxford Street"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") in wartime Britain (December 1944)

Another store to revolutionize the concept of the department store was [Selfridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selfridges "Selfridges") in London, established in 1909 by American-born [Harry Gordon Selfridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Gordon_Selfridge "Harry Gordon Selfridge") on [Oxford Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selfridges,_Oxford_Street "Selfridges, Oxford Street"). The company's marketing promoted the notion of shopping for pleasure rather than necessity, a concept later adopted by department stores worldwide. Dramatic window displays encouraged "just looking".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-33) The store was extensively promoted through paid advertising. The shop floors were structured so that goods could be made more accessible to customers. There were elegant restaurants with modest prices, a library, reading and writing rooms, special reception rooms for French, German, American and "Colonial" customers, a First Aid Room, and a Silence Room, with soft lights, deep chairs, and double-glazing, all intended to keep customers in the store as long as possible. Staff members were taught to be on hand to _assist_ customers, but not too aggressively, and to _sell_ the merchandise.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-34) Selfridge attracted shoppers with educational and scientific exhibits; in 1909, [Louis Blériot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Bl%C3%A9riot "Louis Blériot")'s [monoplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoplane "Monoplane") was exhibited at Selfridges (Blériot was the first to fly over the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel")), and the first public demonstration of television by [John Logie Baird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Logie_Baird "John Logie Baird") took place in the department store in 1925.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/Hiroshige%2C_Sugura_street.jpg/250px-Hiroshige%2C_Sugura_street.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hiroshige,_Sugura_street.jpg)

[Utagawa Hiroshige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utagawa_Hiroshige "Utagawa Hiroshige") designed an [ukiyo-e](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukiyo-e "Ukiyo-e") print with [Mount Fuji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Fuji "Mount Fuji") and Echigoya as landmarks. Echigoya is the former name of Mitsukoshi named after the [former province of Echigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echigo_Province "Echigo Province"). The Mitsukoshi headquarters are located on the left side of the street.

In [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), the first "modern-style" department store was [Mitsukoshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsukoshi "Mitsukoshi"), founded in 1904, which has its root as a [kimono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimono "Kimono") store called Echigoya from 1673. When the roots are considered, however, [Matsuzakaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsuzakaya "Matsuzakaya") has an even longer history, dated from 1611. The kimono store changed to a department store in 1910. In 1924, Matsuzakaya store in [Ginza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginza "Ginza") allowed street shoes to be worn indoors, something innovative at the time.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-35) These former kimono shop department stores dominated the market in its earlier history. They sold, or instead displayed, luxurious products, which contributed to their sophisticated atmospheres. Another origin of the Japanese department store is from [railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway "Railway") companies. There have been many [private railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_railway "Private railway") operators in the nation and, from the 1920s, they started to build department stores directly linked to their lines' [termini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_station#Terminus "Train station"). [Seibu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seibu_Department_Stores "Seibu Department Stores") and [Hankyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hankyu_Department_Stores "Hankyu Department Stores") are typical examples of this type.

### Innovation (1917–1945)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Innovation (1917–1945)")]

In the middle of the 1920s, American management theories such as the [scientific management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_management "Scientific management") of [F.W. Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Winslow_Taylor "Frederick Winslow Taylor") started spreading in Europe. The [International Management Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Management_Institute,_Geneva "International Management Institute, Geneva") (I.M.I.) was established in Geneva in 1927 to facilitate the diffusion of such ideas. A number of department stores teamed up together to create the [International Association of Department Stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Association_of_Department_Stores "International Association of Department Stores") in Paris in 1928 to have a discussion space dedicated to this retail format.

### Expansion to malls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Expansion to malls")]

The U.S. [Baby Boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_Boom "Baby Boom") led to the development of suburban neighborhoods and suburban commercial developments, including shopping malls. Department stores joined these ventures following the growing market of baby boomer spending.

A handful of U.S. retailers had opened seasonal stores in resorts, as well as smaller branch stores in suburbs, in the 1920s and 1930s. Examples include, in [suburban Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Los_Angeles "Greater Los Angeles"), [The Broadway-Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_Hollywood_Building "Broadway Hollywood Building"), [Bullocks Wilshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullocks_Wilshire "Bullocks Wilshire"), The [May Company-Wilshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saban_Building "Saban Building"), [Saks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saks_Fifth_Avenue "Saks Fifth Avenue")-[Beverly Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hills "Beverly Hills"), as well as two [Strawbridge and Clothier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strawbridge_and_Clothier "Strawbridge and Clothier") stores: [Suburban Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburban_Square "Suburban Square") (1930) and [Jenkintown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strawbridge_and_Clothier_Store,_Jenkintown "Strawbridge and Clothier Store, Jenkintown") (1931) outside Philadelphia. Suburban Square was the first shopping center anchored by a department store.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-inq-37) In the 1950s, suburban growth took off – for example, in 1952, [May Company California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_Company_California "May Company California") opened a four-level, 346,700-square-foot (32,210 m 2)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-38) store in [Lakewood Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakewood_Center "Lakewood Center") near Los Angeles, at the time, the largest suburban department store in the world.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-39) However, only three years later it would build an even bigger, 452,000-square-foot (42,000 m 2) store in the [San Fernando Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Fernando_Valley "San Fernando Valley") at [Laurel Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Plaza "Laurel Plaza").

### 2010–today

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2010–today")]

See also: [Retail apocalypse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_apocalypse "Retail apocalypse")

Starting in 2010 many analysts referred to a [retail apocalypse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_apocalypse "Retail apocalypse") in the United States and some other markets, referring to the closing of [brick-and-mortar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick-and-mortar "Brick-and-mortar")[retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail "Retail") stores, especially those of large chains.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-atlantic-41) In 2017, over 12,000 U.S. stores closed due to over-expansion of malls, rising rents, bankruptcies, [leveraged buyouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leveraged_buyout "Leveraged buyout"), low quarterly profits other than during [holiday peak periods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics_of_Christmas "Economics of Christmas"), delayed effects of the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession") of 2008-9,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-atlantic-41) shifts in spending to [experiences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_economy "Experience economy") rather than material goods, relaxed [dress codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_code "Dress code") in workplaces, and the shift to [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce")[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-42) in which [Amazon.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com "Amazon.com") and [Walmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmart "Walmart") dominated versus the online offerings of traditional retailers.

COVID-19 increased the number of permanent store closings in two ways: first through mandatory temporary closing of stores, especially in March and April 2020, with customers largely staying away from stores for non-essential purchases for many more months after that; and secondly, by causing a shift to working from home, which stimulated e-commerce further and reduced demand for business apparel.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Click-and-collect, curbside pickup

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Click-and-collect, curbside pickup")]

[Click-and-collect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnichannel_retail_strategy "Omnichannel retail strategy") services at department stores had been increasing during the 2010s, with many creating larger, distinctly signed, designated areas. Some of the more elaborate ones included features such as reception and seating areas with coffee served, computers with large screens for online shopping, and dressing rooms.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-43)

With the onset of COVID-19 in 2020, most U.S. retailers offered a [curbside pickup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curbside_pickup "Curbside pickup") service as an option on their websites, and a dedicated area at one of the store entrances accessible by car.

### Store-within-a-store

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Store-within-a-store")]

Along with discount stores, mainline department stores implemented more and more "stores-within-a-store". For luxury brands this was often in boutiques similar to the brands' own shops on streets and in malls; they hired their own employees who merchandised the selling space, and rang up the transactions at the brand's own cash registers. The main difference was that the boutique was physically inside the department store building, although in many cases there are walls or windows between the main store space and the boutique, with designated entrances.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Retail establishment

For other uses, see [Department store (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store_(disambiguation) "Department store (disambiguation)").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Bon_March%C3%A9%2C_Paris_-_interior_view.JPG/250px-Bon_March%C3%A9%2C_Paris_-_interior_view.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bon_March%C3%A9,_Paris_-_interior_view.JPG)

Interior of [Le Bon Marché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Bon_March%C3%A9 "Le Bon Marché") in Paris (2008)

A **department store** is a [retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail "Retail") establishment offering a wide range of [consumer goods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_good "Final good") in different areas of the store under one roof, each area ("department") specializing in a product category. In modern major cities, department stores emerged in the mid-19th century, reshaping shopping habits and the definition of service and luxury. Similar developments were under way in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") (with [Whiteleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiteleys "Whiteleys")), in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") ([Le Bon Marché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Bon_March%C3%A9 "Le Bon Marché")) and in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") ([Stewart's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Turney_Stewart "Alexander Turney Stewart")).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-1)

Today, departments often include the following: clothing, cosmetics, [do it yourself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_it_yourself "Do it yourself"), [furniture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furniture "Furniture"), gardening, hardware, [home appliances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_appliance "Home appliance"), [houseware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Household_goods "Household goods"), paint, sporting goods, toiletries, and toys. Additionally, other lines of products such as food, books, jewellery, electronics, [stationery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationery "Stationery"), [photographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photography "Photography") equipment, baby products, and products for pets are sometimes included. Customers generally check out near the front of the store in [discount department stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discount_store "Discount store"), while high-end traditional department stores include sales counters within each department. Some stores are one of many within a larger [retail chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_chain "Retail chain"), while others are independent retailers.

Since the 1980s, department stores have faced increasing competition from discount retailers, and later from [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce") businesses in the 2000s.

## Types

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Types")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Kuopion_Sokos2_-_Haapaniemenkatu_24-26_-_Multim%C3%A4ki_-_Kuopio_-_m.jpg/250px-Kuopion_Sokos2_-_Haapaniemenkatu_24-26_-_Multim%C3%A4ki_-_Kuopio_-_m.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kuopion_Sokos2_-_Haapaniemenkatu_24-26_-_Multim%C3%A4ki_-_Kuopio_-_m.jpg)

[Sokos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sokos "Sokos") department store building in [Multimäki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multim%C3%A4ki "Multimäki"), [Kuopio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuopio "Kuopio"), Finland

Department stores can be classified in several ways:

*   **Mainline department store** or simply, the traditional department store, offering mid- to high-end goods, most or at least some of the time at the full retail price. Examples are [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's"), [Bloomingdale's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomingdale's "Bloomingdale's"), [Nordstrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordstrom "Nordstrom"), [J.C. Penney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J.C._Penney "J.C. Penney"), [Montgomery Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_Ward "Montgomery Ward"), [Sears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears "Sears") and [Belk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belk "Belk").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-2)
    *   **[Junior department store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_department_store "Junior department store")**, a term used principally in the second part of the 20th century for a smaller version of a mainline department store. These were usually either independent stores, or chains such as [Boston Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Store_(California) "Boston Store (California)") and [Harris & Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_&_Frank "Harris & Frank"), which specialized in cosmetics and wearing apparel and accessories, with few home goods.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-4)

*   **Discount department store**, a large [discount store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discount_store "Discount store") selling apparel and home furnishings at a discount, either selling overstock from mainline department stores, or merchandise especially made for the discount department store market. Examples are [Nordstrom Rack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordstrom_Rack "Nordstrom Rack"), [Saks Off 5th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saks_Off_5th "Saks Off 5th"), [Marshalls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshalls "Marshalls"), [Ross Dress for Less](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Dress_for_Less "Ross Dress for Less"), [TJ Maxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TJ_Maxx "TJ Maxx"), and [Kohl's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kohl's "Kohl's").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-mainline-5)

Some sources may refer to the following types of stores as department stores, even though they are not generally considered as such:

*   [Hypermarkets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypermarket "Hypermarket") (discount superstores with full grocery offerings, such as [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation "Target Corporation"), [Walmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmart "Walmart") and [Carrefour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrefour "Carrefour"))[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-6)
*   [Variety stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_store "Variety store"), also known in the U.S. as [five and dimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_and_dime "Five and dime"), or dollar stores

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

### Origins in England, 1700s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Origins in England, 1700s")]

One of the first department stores may have been Bennett's in [Derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby "Derby"), first established as an [ironmonger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironmonger "Ironmonger") (hardware shop) in 1734.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-Bennetts-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-derbyshire-8) It continued trading in the same building until its administration and closure in 2019.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-Bennetts-7) However, the first reliably dated department store to be established, was [Harding, Howell & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harding,_Howell_&_Co. "Harding, Howell & Co."), which opened in 1796 on [Pall Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pall_Mall,_London "Pall Mall, London"), London.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-9) The oldest department store chain may be [Debenhams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debenhams "Debenhams"), which was established in 1778 and closed in 2021. It is the longest trading defunct British retailer. An observer writing in _[Ackermann's Repository](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ackermann's\_Repository "Ackermann's Repository")_, a British periodical on contemporary taste and fashion, described the enterprise in 1809 as follows:

> The house is one hundred and fifty feet in length from front to back, and of proportionate width. It is fitted up with great taste, and is divided by glazed partitions into four departments, for the various branches of the extensive business, which is there carried on. Immediately at the entrance is the first department, which is exclusively appropriated to the sale of furs and fans. The second contains articles of haberdashery of every description, silks, muslins, lace, gloves, &etc. In the third shop, on the right, you meet with a rich assortment of jewelry, ornamental articles in ormolu, French clocks, &etc.; and on the left, with all the different kinds of perfumery necessary for the toilette. The fourth is set apart for millinery and dresses; so that there is no article of female attire or decoration, but what may be here procured in the first style of elegance and fashion. This concern has been conducted for the last twelve years by the present proprietors who have spared neither trouble nor expense to ensure the establishment of a superiority over every other in Europe, and to render it perfectly unique in its kind.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-10)

This venture is described as having all of the basic characteristics of the department store; it was a public retail establishment offering a wide range of [consumer goods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_good "Consumer good") in different departments. Jonathan Glancey for the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") writes:

> Harding, Howell & Co was focused on the needs and desires of fashionable women. Here, at last women were free to browse and shop, safely and decorously, away from home and from the company of men. These, for the main part, were newly affluent middle-class women, their good fortune – and the department store itself – nurtured and shaped by the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"). This was transforming life in London and the length and breadth of Britain at a dizzying pace on the back of energetic free trade, fecund invention, steam and sail, and a seemingly inexhaustible supply of expendable cheap labour.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-11)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Harrod%27s_%2850718173793%29.jpg/250px-Harrod%27s_%2850718173793%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harrod's_(50718173793).jpg)

[Harrods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrods "Harrods") illuminated exterior at night in Knightsbridge, London

This pioneering shop was closed down in 1820 when the [business partnership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_partnership "Business partnership") was dissolved. By the mid-to-late nineteenth century, most major [High Streets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Street "High Street") in British cities featured flourishing department stores. Increasingly, women became the main customers.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-12)[Kendals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendals "Kendals") (formerly Kendal Milne & Faulkner) in Manchester lays claim to being one of the first department stores and is still known to many of its customers as Kendal's, despite its 2005 name change to [House of Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Fraser "House of Fraser"). The Manchester institution dates back to 1836 but had been trading as Watts Bazaar since 1796.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-PB80-13) At its zenith the store had buildings on both sides of Deansgate linked by a subterranean passage "Kendals Arcade" and an art nouveau tiled food hall. The store was especially known for its emphasis on quality and style over low prices giving it the nickname "the Harrods of the North", although this was due in part to Harrods acquiring the store in 1919. [Harrods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrods "Harrods") of London can be traced back to 1834, though the current store was built between 1894 and 1905. Opened in 1830, [Austins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austins_(department_store) "Austins (department store)") in Derry remained in operation as the world's oldest independent department store until its closure in 2016.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-15)[Lewis's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis's "Lewis's") of Liverpool operated from 1856 to 2010. A concept devised by retail entrepreneur [David Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lewis_(English_merchant) "David Lewis (English merchant)"), the world's first [Christmas grotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa's_workshop "Santa's workshop") opened in Lewis's in 1879, entitled 'Christmas Fairyland'.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-16)[Liberty & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_(department_store) "Liberty (department store)") in London's [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_of_London "West End of London") gained popularity in the 1870s for selling Oriental goods.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-17) In 1889, [Oscar Wilde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Wilde "Oscar Wilde") wrote "Liberty's is the chosen resort of the artistic shopper".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-18)

### Origins in Parisian _magasins de nouveautés_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Origins in Parisian magasins de nouveautés")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/Au_Bon_March%C3%A9_%28vue_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_-_gravure%29.jpg/250px-Au_Bon_March%C3%A9_%28vue_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_-_gravure%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Au_Bon_March%C3%A9_(vue_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_-_gravure).jpg)

Au Bon Marché

The Paris department stores have roots in the _magasin de nouveautés_, or [novelty stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_store?action=edit&redlink=1 "Novelty store (page does not exist)"); the first, the Tapis Rouge, was created in 1784.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-19) They flourished in the early 19th century. [Balzac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balzac "Balzac") described their functioning in his novel _[César Birotteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar\_Birotteau "César Birotteau")_. In the 1840s, with the arrival of the railroads in Paris and the increased number of shoppers they brought, they grew, and began to have large plate glass display windows, fixed prices and price tags, and advertising in newspapers.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-Fierro_(1996),_pages_911%E2%80%93912-20)

A novelty shop called _[Au Bon Marché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_Bon\_March%C3%A9 "Le Bon Marché")_ was founded in Paris in 1838 to sell items like lace, ribbons, sheets, mattresses, buttons, and umbrellas. It grew from 300 m 2 (3,200 ft 2) and 12 employees in 1838 to 50,000 m 2 (540,000 ft 2) and 1,788 employees in 1879. Boucicaut was renowned for his marketing innovations; a reading room for husbands while their wives shopped; extensive newspaper advertising; entertainment for children; and six million catalogues sent out to customers. By 1880 half the employees were women; unmarried women employees lived in dormitories on the upper floors.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-world-21)

_Au Bon Marché_ soon had [Printemps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printemps "Printemps"), founded in 1865; [La Samaritaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Samaritaine "La Samaritaine") (1869), Bazar de Hotel de Ville ([BHV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bazar_de_l'H%C3%B4tel_de_Ville "Bazar de l'Hôtel de Ville")); and [Galeries Lafayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galeries_Lafayette "Galeries Lafayette") (1895) as competitors.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-Fierro_(1996),_pages_911%E2%80%93912-20)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-22) The French gloried the national prestige brought by the Parisian stores.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-Heidrun_Homburg_1992_pp_183-219-23)[Émile Zola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Zola "Émile Zola") (1840–1902) set his novel _[Au Bonheur des Dames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au\_Bonheur\_des\_Dames "Au Bonheur des Dames")_ (1882–83) in the typical department store, making it a symbol of the new technology that was improving society and devouring it.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-24)

### First Australian department stores

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: First Australian department stores")]

Australia is notable for having the longest continuously operating department store, [David Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Jones_(department_store) "David Jones (department store)").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-:0-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-26) The first David Jones department store was opened on 24 May 1838, by Welsh born immigrant David Jones in a "large and commodious premises" on the corner of [George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Street,_Sydney "George Street, Sydney") and [Barrack Streets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrack_Street "Barrack Street") in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), only 50 years after the foundation of the colony. Expanding to a number of stores in the various states of Australia, David Jones is the oldest continuously operating department franchise in the world.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-:0-25) Other department stores in Australia include [Grace Bros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Bros "Grace Bros") founded in 1885, now merged with [Myer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myer "Myer") which was founded in 1900.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-27)

### First American department stores (1825–1858)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: First American department stores (1825–1858)")]

[Arnold Constable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Constable_&_Company "Arnold Constable & Company") was the first American department store. It was founded in 1825 as a small dry goods store on Pine Street in New York City. In 1857 the store moved into a five-story white marble dry goods palace known as the Marble House. During the Civil War, Arnold Constable was one of the first stores to issue charge bills of credit to its customers each month instead of on a bi-annual basis. The store soon outgrew the Marble House and erected a cast-iron building on Broadway and Nineteenth Street in 1869; this "Palace of Trade" expanded over the years until it was necessary to move into a larger space in 1914. Financial problems led to bankruptcy in 1975.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-28)

In New York City in 1846, [Alexander Turney Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Turney_Stewart "Alexander Turney Stewart") established the "[Marble Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/280_Broadway "280 Broadway")" on [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(Manhattan) "Broadway (Manhattan)"), between Chambers and Reade streets. He offered European retail merchandise at fixed prices on a variety of dry goods, and advertised a policy of providing "free entrance" to all potential customers. Though it was clad in white marble to look like a [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance")[palazzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo "Palazzo"), the building's [cast iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cast_iron "Cast iron") construction permitted large [plate glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_glass "Plate glass") windows that permitted major seasonal displays, especially in the Christmas shopping season. In 1862, Stewart built a new store on a full city block uptown between 9th and 10th streets, with eight floors. His innovations included buying from manufacturers for cash and in large quantities, keeping his markup small and prices low, truthful presentation of merchandise, the one-price policy (so there was no haggling), simple merchandise returns and cash refund policy, selling for cash and not credit, buyers who searched worldwide for quality merchandise, departmentalization, vertical and horizontal integration, volume sales, and free services for customers such as waiting rooms and free delivery of purchases.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-29) In 1858, [Rowland Hussey Macy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowland_Hussey_Macy "Rowland Hussey Macy") founded [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's") as a dry goods store.

### Innovations 1850–1917

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Innovations 1850–1917")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Marshall_field_interior.jpg/250px-Marshall_field_interior.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marshall_field_interior.jpg)

Marshall Field's State Street store "great hall" interior around 1910

[Marshall Field & Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Field's "Marshall Field's") originated in 1852. It was the premier department store on the busiest shopping street in the Midwest at the time, [State Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Street_(Chicago) "State Street (Chicago)") in Chicago.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-30) Marshall Field's was often cited as a model for other department stores in that it had exceptional customer service.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Marshall Field's also had the firsts; among many innovations by Marshall Field's were the first European buying office, which was located in Manchester, England, and the first bridal registry. The company was the first to introduce the concept of the personal shopper, and that service was provided without charge in every Field's store, until the chain's last days under the Marshall Field's name. It was the first store to offer revolving credit and the first department store to use [escalators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escalator "Escalator").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Marshall Field's book department in the State Street store was legendary;[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] it pioneered the concept of the "book signing". Moreover, every year at Christmas, Marshall Field's downtown store windows were filled with animated displays as part of the downtown shopping district display; the "theme" window displays became famous for their ingenuity and beauty, and visiting the Marshall Field's windows at Christmas became a tradition for Chicagoans and visitors alike, as popular a local practice as visiting the Walnut Room with its equally famous Christmas tree or meeting "under the clock" on State Street.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-31)

In 1877, [John Wanamaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wanamaker "John Wanamaker") opened what some claim was the United States' first "modern" department store in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"): the first to offer fixed prices marked on every article and also introduced electrical illumination (1878), the telephone (1879), and the use of pneumatic tubes to transport cash and documents (1880) to the department store business.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-32)

Aerial view of [Anthony Hordern & Sons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Hordern_&_Sons "Anthony Hordern & Sons") in [Sydney, Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney,_Australia "Sydney, Australia") (1936), once the largest department store in the world

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Christmas_Party_For_Trooper_Devereux%27s_Daughter-_Christmas_in_Wartime%2C_Pinner%2C_Middlesex%2C_December_1944_D23005.jpg/250px-Christmas_Party_For_Trooper_Devereux%27s_Daughter-_Christmas_in_Wartime%2C_Pinner%2C_Middlesex%2C_December_1944_D23005.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Christmas_Party_For_Trooper_Devereux's_Daughter-_Christmas_in_Wartime,_Pinner,_Middlesex,_December_1944_D23005.jpg)

[Selfridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selfridges "Selfridges") in [Oxford Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Street "Oxford Street"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") in wartime Britain (December 1944)

Another store to revolutionize the concept of the department store was [Selfridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selfridges "Selfridges") in London, established in 1909 by American-born [Harry Gordon Selfridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Gordon_Selfridge "Harry Gordon Selfridge") on [Oxford Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selfridges,_Oxford_Street "Selfridges, Oxford Street"). The company's marketing promoted the notion of shopping for pleasure rather than necessity, a concept later adopted by department stores worldwide. Dramatic window displays encouraged "just looking".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-33) The store was extensively promoted through paid advertising. The shop floors were structured so that goods could be made more accessible to customers. There were elegant restaurants with modest prices, a library, reading and writing rooms, special reception rooms for French, German, American and "Colonial" customers, a First Aid Room, and a Silence Room, with soft lights, deep chairs, and double-glazing, all intended to keep customers in the store as long as possible. Staff members were taught to be on hand to _assist_ customers, but not too aggressively, and to _sell_ the merchandise.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-34) Selfridge attracted shoppers with educational and scientific exhibits; in 1909, [Louis Blériot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Bl%C3%A9riot "Louis Blériot")'s [monoplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoplane "Monoplane") was exhibited at Selfridges (Blériot was the first to fly over the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel")), and the first public demonstration of television by [John Logie Baird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Logie_Baird "John Logie Baird") took place in the department store in 1925.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/Hiroshige%2C_Sugura_street.jpg/250px-Hiroshige%2C_Sugura_street.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hiroshige,_Sugura_street.jpg)

[Utagawa Hiroshige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utagawa_Hiroshige "Utagawa Hiroshige") designed an [ukiyo-e](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukiyo-e "Ukiyo-e") print with [Mount Fuji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Fuji "Mount Fuji") and Echigoya as landmarks. Echigoya is the former name of Mitsukoshi named after the [former province of Echigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echigo_Province "Echigo Province"). The Mitsukoshi headquarters are located on the left side of the street.

In [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), the first "modern-style" department store was [Mitsukoshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitsukoshi "Mitsukoshi"), founded in 1904, which has its root as a [kimono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimono "Kimono") store called Echigoya from 1673. When the roots are considered, however, [Matsuzakaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsuzakaya "Matsuzakaya") has an even longer history, dated from 1611. The kimono store changed to a department store in 1910. In 1924, Matsuzakaya store in [Ginza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginza "Ginza") allowed street shoes to be worn indoors, something innovative at the time.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-35) These former kimono shop department stores dominated the market in its earlier history. They sold, or instead displayed, luxurious products, which contributed to their sophisticated atmospheres. Another origin of the Japanese department store is from [railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway "Railway") companies. There have been many [private railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_railway "Private railway") operators in the nation and, from the 1920s, they started to build department stores directly linked to their lines' [termini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_station#Terminus "Train station"). [Seibu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seibu_Department_Stores "Seibu Department Stores") and [Hankyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hankyu_Department_Stores "Hankyu Department Stores") are typical examples of this type.

### Innovation (1917–1945)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Innovation (1917–1945)")]

In the middle of the 1920s, American management theories such as the [scientific management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_management "Scientific management") of [F.W. Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Winslow_Taylor "Frederick Winslow Taylor") started spreading in Europe. The [International Management Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Management_Institute,_Geneva "International Management Institute, Geneva") (I.M.I.) was established in Geneva in 1927 to facilitate the diffusion of such ideas. A number of department stores teamed up together to create the [International Association of Department Stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Association_of_Department_Stores "International Association of Department Stores") in Paris in 1928 to have a discussion space dedicated to this retail format.

### Expansion to malls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Expansion to malls")]

[![Image 13: [icon]](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg/20px-Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg)This section **needs expansion**. You can help by [adding missing information](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=). _(October 2020)_

The U.S. [Baby Boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_Boom "Baby Boom") led to the development of suburban neighborhoods and suburban commercial developments, including shopping malls. Department stores joined these ventures following the growing market of baby boomer spending.

A handful of U.S. retailers had opened seasonal stores in resorts, as well as smaller branch stores in suburbs, in the 1920s and 1930s. Examples include, in [suburban Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Los_Angeles "Greater Los Angeles"), [The Broadway-Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_Hollywood_Building "Broadway Hollywood Building"), [Bullocks Wilshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullocks_Wilshire "Bullocks Wilshire"), The [May Company-Wilshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saban_Building "Saban Building"), [Saks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saks_Fifth_Avenue "Saks Fifth Avenue")-[Beverly Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hills "Beverly Hills"), as well as two [Strawbridge and Clothier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strawbridge_and_Clothier "Strawbridge and Clothier") stores: [Suburban Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburban_Square "Suburban Square") (1930) and [Jenkintown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strawbridge_and_Clothier_Store,_Jenkintown "Strawbridge and Clothier Store, Jenkintown") (1931) outside Philadelphia. Suburban Square was the first shopping center anchored by a department store.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-inq-37) In the 1950s, suburban growth took off – for example, in 1952, [May Company California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_Company_California "May Company California") opened a four-level, 346,700-square-foot (32,210 m 2)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-38) store in [Lakewood Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakewood_Center "Lakewood Center") near Los Angeles, at the time, the largest suburban department store in the world.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-39) However, only three years later it would build an even bigger, 452,000-square-foot (42,000 m 2) store in the [San Fernando Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Fernando_Valley "San Fernando Valley") at [Laurel Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_Plaza "Laurel Plaza").

### 2010–today

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2010–today")]

See also: [Retail apocalypse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_apocalypse "Retail apocalypse")

Starting in 2010 many analysts referred to a [retail apocalypse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_apocalypse "Retail apocalypse") in the United States and some other markets, referring to the closing of [brick-and-mortar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick-and-mortar "Brick-and-mortar")[retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail "Retail") stores, especially those of large chains.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-atlantic-41) In 2017, over 12,000 U.S. stores closed due to over-expansion of malls, rising rents, bankruptcies, [leveraged buyouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leveraged_buyout "Leveraged buyout"), low quarterly profits other than during [holiday peak periods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics_of_Christmas "Economics of Christmas"), delayed effects of the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession") of 2008-9,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-atlantic-41) shifts in spending to [experiences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_economy "Experience economy") rather than material goods, relaxed [dress codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_code "Dress code") in workplaces, and the shift to [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce")[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-42) in which [Amazon.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com "Amazon.com") and [Walmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmart "Walmart") dominated versus the online offerings of traditional retailers.

COVID-19 increased the number of permanent store closings in two ways: first through mandatory temporary closing of stores, especially in March and April 2020, with customers largely staying away from stores for non-essential purchases for many more months after that; and secondly, by causing a shift to working from home, which stimulated e-commerce further and reduced demand for business apparel.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Click-and-collect, curbside pickup

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Click-and-collect, curbside pickup")]

[Click-and-collect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnichannel_retail_strategy "Omnichannel retail strategy") services at department stores had been increasing during the 2010s, with many creating larger, distinctly signed, designated areas. Some of the more elaborate ones included features such as reception and seating areas with coffee served, computers with large screens for online shopping, and dressing rooms.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_store#cite_note-43)

With the onset of COVID-19 in 2020, most U.S. retailers offered a [curbside pickup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curbside_pickup "Curbside pickup") service as an option on their websites, and a dedicated area at one of the store entrances accessible by car.

### Store-within-a-store

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Department_store&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Store-within-a-store")]

Along with discount stores, mainline department stores implemented more and more "stores-within-a-store". For luxury brands this was often in boutiques similar to the brands' own shops on streets and in malls; they hired their own employees who merchandised the selling space, and rang up the transactions at the brand's own cash registers. The main difference was that the boutique was physically inside the department store building, although in many cases there are walls or windows between the main store space and the boutique, with designated entrances.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
