### CHAPTER XXXIX. - THE CITY OF LE MARS.

Forty-six years ago the present site of the beautiful little city of Le Mars was but a wild prairie, with the babbling waters of the Floyd river coursing through. The town was brought into existence in 1870 through the building of the railroad from Dubuque to Sioux City, by the Dubuque & Sioux City Railroad Company, and was at first styled “St. Paul Junction.” It was platted by John I. Blair, and officers of the railroad corporation, June 4, 1870. It was not named, however, until the following September, when a party made up of John I. Blair and family, W. W. Walker, of Cedar Rapids; Mrs. John Weare, Mr. and Mrs. Swain and Mrs. Parsons, of Fort Dodge; Mr. and Mrs. Dr. William R. Smith of Sioux City; Mrs. John Cleghorn, Sioux City; Colonel Wayne, of New York, and Anable, of Iowa, with Mrs. Reynolds, of Clinton, Iowa, and Mrs. Underhill, of New York, came by special train to sections 9 and 16, in township 90, range 45, west. The town was named by the ladies of the party taking the initials of their names, and so arranging them as to produce a name truly befitting. after much “combining work” the letters were so adjusted as to produce the pretty name, Le Mars.

When the first settlers of this county settled along the Floyd and Big Sioux rivers in 1856-57, with a few more who had found their way here by the time of the awful Indian massacre in Minnesota, in the summer of 1862, the land where Le Mars stands was the habitation of wild birds of passage and the nimble-footed elk and deer, and was disturbed only by some hunter or scout of the white race, or by Indians roving in search of game and suitable camping places.

In 1866 – the year after the Civil War ended – that noble old pioneer, Captain B. F. Bettsworth, moved to the site where Le Mars now stands and erected a log cabin, forty rods from where the Gehlen flour-mill subsequently stood, on the banks of the Floyd. Captain Bettsworth's family consisted of a wife, ten sons and four daughters.

The same season came in Amos Martin and J. P. Ladd, making their settlement. As Captain Bettsworth once remarked: “love was then known without the Eden serpent; to ask a favor was to receive; the sorrow of one household became thee grief of all, and the joy of one was but gladness to all within the limits of thee little settlement on the Floyd.”

Le Mars was made the county seat in 1872 by a county election, at which the vote stood 476 to 111. The land occupied by the plat, was originally owned by Captain Bettsworth, Jerry Ladd and Amos Martin. Captain Betsworth had claimed that portion located in section 9, in 1866, and finally exchanged it for three times its acreage, with the Iowa Falls & Sioux City Railroad Company, which desired it for townsite purposes, as it has already been determined that here was to be the junction of the present Illinois Central and the Chicago, St. Paul, Minneapolis & Omaha railroads.

SOME IMPORTANT FIRST EVENTS.

The first actual settler on the townsite of Le Mars was Capt. B. F. Betsworth. Date 1866.

The first child born of white parents in this vicinity was the grandson of Captain Betsworth and wife, born to their son, John H. Betsworth and wife.

Aside from the humble willow cabin built by Captain Betsworth on his original claim, the first house was erected by J. P. Ladd, on lots later used by Mr. Perry for his coal yard. The house was sold to David Gibbs and removed.

The first railroad was the Iowa Falls & Sioux City railroad (now the Illinois Central line), which came in 1869.

The first church edifice was that of the Methodist Episcopal congregation, built in 1873. That church society, however, had been organized in 1869.

The first school house was built just south of the original plat, in section 17, in which John H. Betsworth taught the pioneer school. The first school building on the plat was erected in 1870, a two-story frame structure, which was finally sold and used for church purposes.

The first newspaper was the _Plymouth Sentinel,_ the first number of which was issued on December 22, 1870, and which later became known as the _Le Mars Semi-Weekly Sentinel._

RECOLLECTIONS OF EARLY DAYS.

The “History of the Town of Le Mars,” printed as a small booklet in Des Moines, in 1871, has the following:

“Fifteen months ago the ground upon which the town now stands was unbroken prairie, with the exception of land owned by Jerry P. Ladd, which was a partly-cultivated farm, which he soon sold to the railroad company. There was only one white man settled within sight of the place three years ago; this was Captain Betsworth, and his nearest neighbor was several miles down the valley, in the direction of Sioux City The town was platted in December, 1869, but no lots were offered for sale until June, 1870, and the place now boasts of four hundred inhabitants.

“The business lots are twenty-four by one hundred feet, and range in price from one hundred and fifty to three hundred dollars each.

“There are two dry goods stores; three grocery and provision stores; one drug store; one hardware store; one boot and shoe store; lumber and coal yards, two; blacksmith shops, two; harness, one; meat markets, two; barber shop, one; hotels, three; land officers, two; millinery and dressmaker's shop, one. There are two doctors and two lawyers; a school of fifty scholars, one church – Catholic – and a grist mill half a mile away.

“THE FLOUR MILL.

“was built so as to commence business on the last of November, 1870. This brought the farmers to the place with grist from southern Minnesota and Dakota Territory, a distance of seventy miles and more. A large portion of the customers of the mill have been much disappointed, not on account of courtesy on the part of the mill-owners, but on account of the low stage of water in the river Floyd, by reason of which not more than one-eighth of the capacity of the mill can be utilized. A steam flouring-mill would be a great boon to the place, and there is probably no better place in Northwestern Iowa, where it would pay better to erect a mill, than at Le Mars. A grain elevator is also much needed and will pay. These are two things the people of this section of Iowa must have, as there has been a large quantity of prairie broken the last year, which, with a few yields of crops, will afford business for ten run of stones.”

This sounds odd to the people here now, in the shadow of the largest roller-mill in all Iowa, where fourteen hundred barrels of “Plymouth” flour are turned out daily and have been for many years.

AS RECALLED BY CAPTAIN BETSWORTH.

When in a reminiscent mood, one time back in 1893, Captain Betsworth, pioneer settler in this vicinity, related how in 1866 he built his humble cabin on the banks of the Floyd river, just east of the present wagon bridge. He said for many months the only water his family used was that obtained from the waters of the Floyd, which was “plenty cold” in the winter and “plenty warm” in the summer months. But one day Betsworth set out on a pure-water expedition and not far from the “big tree,” near where stood Gehlen's old mill, in the northern part of Le Mars, he found a small spring and, going to the house, he procured a spade and set a barrel in the spring and before many hours the barrel was running over with clear cool, soft spring water.

It was at this point that the Winnebago Indians used to come and camp in those days. On their spring and autumn hunting expeditions, scores, and sometimes hundreds, would camp on either side of the stream. The captain once told the writer how, in 1866, a large band of Indians consisting of many complete families camped here and crossed the stream on a willow foot-log, which his sons had thrown across the stream. Upon one occasion, after an unsuccessful hunt away up in Lyon and Sioux counties, these Indians came back half starved and wanted food. Captain Betsworth generally turned none away, but this time they were too numerous. He had just harvested a large crop of potatoes, which he had placed in a root cellar. near this he had thrown out many small potatoes and there were also a number of half-rotten summer squashes lying on the ground. he told the Indians they might have these. They at once commenced picking them up and eating them raw. This beat all kinds of human diet the good Captain had ever seen before.

This was four years previous to the platting of Le Mars and the deer and elk, as well as other wild game, abounded hereabout. There were several Indian burials near the cottonwood trees where now stands the northern portion of the present city of Le Mars. These burials were made at about the close of the Civil War. The clump of cottonwood trees could be seen towering up from out the prairies a great distance, as far down the Floyd valley as the point where Hinton now stands. The Indian wigwams are gone – Captain Betsworth has long since been numbered among the dead – and the “big trees” have all succumbed to the ravages of time, save one, which stands still as a sentinel of those long—ago pioneer years in this county. Who can conjecture what scenes will present themselves to view here when another half century has gone?

POPULATION OF LE MARS.

In November, 1891, Le Mars was classed as the third city in Iowa for having made the greatest gain in population during the decade between 1880 and 1890. The United States census returns placed Sioux City at the head, that city having increased at a greater rate than any other Iowa city during that decade. Des Moines was second, while Le Mars was third, having made an increase of almost one hundred and thirteen per cent. In 18800 the city had a population of 1895, and in the next ten-year period it contained 4,036 population. There were then fourteen passenger trains daily in and out of the city; two large flour mills, fourteen hotels, twelve churches, four banks, a waterworks system, an electric light plant, a gas-lighting plant, fine public schools and a normal school.

The population of the city, according to the 1915 state census, was 5,070. The same authority gives the population at various dates as follow: In 1885 the city had 3,808; in 1890, 4,036; in 1895, 5,046; in 1900, 4,146; in 1905, 5,041, and in 1910, 4,157.

THE LE MARS POSTOFFICE.

A postoffice was established at Le Mars in 1869, with John Bloget as the first postmaster. Blogett & Foster kept a general store and in this the postoffice was kept. It was situated in the extreme western part of the town, as then constituted. From “Deacon” Blodgett, the postoffice went to Charles Aldrich, who held the position six years. The next postmaster was Col. J. M. Emery, who also served six years and was succeeded by J. F. Vogt, who removed the office to the east side of Main street, where it was kept in the nineties. Vogt held the post office through a part of President Cleveland's administration and until January 20, 1889, in President Harrison's administration, when the office was given to A. P. Brown, a disabled Union soldier, who held the position until Cleveland was again President, after which it was turned over to A. Thoma, who was succeeded, under President McKinley's administration, by Phil A. Boland. The next postmaster was W. S. Freeman, who held the office for nine years and was succeeded by J. E. Kelley, who was appointed under the administration of President Woodrow Wilson.

Up to June, 1890, there had been money orders issued from this office to the number of $43,835; also postal notes to the number of 22,775. The first money order issued from the Le Mars postoffice was issued to James Arthur, to be paid to Booge & Company, Sioux City, for the sum of $4.25.

The present number of rural free delivery routes is nine; number of employees in office, six; number of city carriers, four. The total receipts of the office for the last quarter, ending September 1, 1916, was $19,031.03.

The present government postoffice building came after a long-delayed pull, but it is a fine, modern structure, of which any small city may be justly proud. The contract was let on August 25, 1914, and the building was to be finished by the end of fifteen months from that date. It is constructed of light gray pressed brick, with dark red limestone trimmings. The contract was let to the Herman Construction Company of St. Louis, Missouri. The price paid was $45,370 for the naked building and it cost $4,630 to put in the necessary interior furnishings. The postoffice stands on the corner of Court and Seventh streets. It was completed and first occupied on January 1, 1916. The surrounding grounds are beautifully parked and have cement walks and driveways for the rural mail wagons, as well as for transporting the mail to and from the railroad station a block to the east. A stately flag staff was provided for the southwest corner of the postoffice block, and, waving over the beautiful public building, daily may be seen the national colors.

The ground on which the postoffice stands was formerly known as the Staples property and was owned by the Plymouth Brewing Company, which sold thee ground to the government for three thousand dollars.

The postoffice was robbed in 1894 of five hundred dollars in money and eight hundred dollars in postage stamps.

PROVISIONS FOR A CITY HALL.

In 1888 the city bonded itself in the sum of ten thousand dollars, for ten years, at six per cent. interest, to raise funds with which to provide a fire-engine and obtain a suitable city hall. It purchased the two-story brick block, at the southeast corner of Main and Seventh streets, which had been erected for a business house. The price paid was five thousand dollars, and a thousand dollars more was expended in addition. The city officers, fire-engine house, hose carts and the like were to be kept therein, while the front part of the building, for a time, was leased for business uses and the second story for a printing office. In the nineties, however, the whole building was used by the city, and in it the public library was kept and the council rooms were removed to the upper story; while a jail was provided underneath the building, same as today, except that the public library is now housed in a fine building erected exclusively for that purpose.

In 1883 a fire steamer was bought for three thousand eight hundred dollars, by which the city was protected from the ravages of fires. Twenty-five years later the city secured the water it needed from the private waterworks system, then owned by J. H. Winchel, paying the sum of two thousand four hundred dollars a year water rent. In the fall of 1916 the city purchased an improved auto-truck, carrying a large chemical engine, and costing twenty-seven hundred dollars. It is claimed that this machine has already more than paid for itself in property saved since it was installed.

The city of Le Mars now has a bonded indebtedness of sixteen thousand dollars; has five miles of paved streets; nearly a hundred miles of cement walks, beautiful boulevard lights for street lighting; a volunteer fire company of forty or more well-drilled men, and an ample amount of good hose and hook-and-ladder appliances.

In 1916 the officers of the city are: Mayor, Frank J. Smith; alderman from First ward, N. B. Bryant; Second, J. F. Beattie; Third, A. P. Dornbusch; alderman-at-large, J. V. Herker and E. E. Eastman; treasurer, Andrew Langhout; solicitor, Herbert S. Martin; clerk, E. F. Parker; assessor, C. L. Pinney; civil engineer, B. C. Woolley; street commissioner, William Deviney; chief of police, Barney Sudmeyer; night watchmen, J. O'Rourke and John Boyle.

COMMERCIAL INTERESTS OF THE CITY.

The completion of the Illinois Central railway and the building of the depot in the autumn of 1869 marked the beginning of the commercial development of the present thriving city of Le Mars, long ago styled “the Gateway City.”

The pioneer general-merchandise store was operated by Deacon John Blodget and O. b. Foster, in 1869, under the firm title of Blodget & Foster. It was situated in the extreme western part of the place, where the dairy farm was located later. There the first postoffice was kept, Mr. Blodget being Le Mar's first postmaster.

The first to embark in trade along the present business street was a groceryman named John Gordon, who, in 1869, located on the corner of Court and Seventh streets. He subsequently sold to Mr. Fairchild.

A drug store was opened by Charles Bennett on the lot where no stands the German-American Savings Bank (old site of the First National Bank). A hardware store was put in by Orson Bennett just north of the bank.

A saloon was started by W. W. Johnson, at the corner of Sixth and Main streets. C. G. Norris started the first meat market in 1870, on the lot now occupied by Julius Schmidt, at the corner of Main and Sixth streets.

THE CITY'S HOTEL INTERESTS.

The first hotel was the Dubuque House, kept by Charles Hoffman. A Mr. Wood built and conducted the St. Cloud Hotel – better known as “Neck Roast,” on account of the inferior meats served. This latter hotel in later years was turned into a boarding house.

The Revere House was built by Mrs. Atkinson, who, with her son-in-law, operated it at first. It stood on the present site of the Union House, and was burned on July 25, 1884, by incendiaries. James Murphy served several years in the state prison as one of the guilty parties. At the time the building was burned it belonged to Monahan & Wilson, but the hotel was conducted by A. Brown.

The Depot Hotel was prominent among the early hotels of Le Mars. It was erected by the railroad company, upon the completion of the Illinois Central road, and served as a station-house, hotel and residence for the local agent, who was usually the landlord in charge. The first landlord to serve was L. K. Bowman, who was shortly succeeded by Col. J. M. Emery. In May, 1878, the house was burned, the fire being started by the explosion of a faulty kerosene lamp.

In 1887 a stock company was formed of home capital and the present splendid Union Hotel was erected on the lot where had stood the old Revere House. The Union Hotel is a three-story brick structure, located at the corner of Sixth and Eagle streets, and has always enjoyed a good patronage. It is now, and has been for years, conducted by Ben Hodgeman, a natural-born landlord, whose eyes are ever open to the wants of his guests.

SOME EARLY MERCANTILE ENTERPRISES.

Among the many early-day changes in business may be named the fact that C. P. Woodard bought out John Blodget's agricultural business and George Walton sold his grocery business to George Carter.

Roe Amsden's grocery, corner of Main and Seventh streets, was blown down by the great wind storm of 1870.

The first lumberman at Le Mars was Wesley Young. The first to handle millinery goods was Mrs. Milliman. De Witt Clarke established the first exclusive hardware store in the place, about the spring of 1873. Spring Brothers opened up a big store in the same line and for many years were the heaviest dealers of the place. The first farm implements were sold by Deacon John Blodget.

Henry Van Sickle built the block later owned and occupied by Pew Brothers, as a store for their hardware and farm implements.

Amsden's Hall, over the store building at the corner of Main and Seventh streets, was the first public hall, and it was used for the early courts, religious meetings, and general public assemblies.

W. H. Smith was the pioneer merchant tailor. He came in 1872.

The first banking house was opened in 1871 by Rymer & Kent. It was styled the Le Mars Bank.

In 1875 there were shipped from Le Mars eight hundred and eleven carloads of wheat. From the autumn of 1883 to the autumn of 1884 there were shipped out of Le Mars twenty-four hundred and sixty-eight cars of produce, and during the same period there were nineteen hundred and ten cars of merchandise received.

The pioneer newspaper was the _“Sentinel,”_ established by J. C. Buchanan in 1870. His office was located where later the Mickley Hotel stood. Most of the residents paid for two copies for two years in advance in order to get the paper started.

In 1870 Peter Gehlen's flour-mill was erected on the bank of the Floyd river. The proprietor boarded at the home of the pioneer, Captain Betsworth, while looking for a site for his mill. The good Captain, who was a ship-carpenter by trade, assisted him in constructing his dam.

DALTON'S OPERA HOUSE.

Dalton's Opera House, occupying a good location of Sixth street, was built in 1884 by H. L. Hoyt and John Draudt, at an expense of fifty-five thousand dollars, inclusive of the ten-thousand-dollar lot on which it stands. In 1877 the property passed into the hands of the banker, P. F. Dalton. It has a seating capacity of twelve hundred people. In the same year in which Mr. Dalton bought the property he leased to the Masonic fraternity, for lodge rooms purposes, the southwest corner.

SOME EARLY HAPPENINGS.

In 1871 there were only about forty souls in the vicinity of Le Mars and only one hundred and six acres of land broken. There were only eight votes polled at the first election. The first school house was erected by G. M. Bolser and D. M. Herman. Mr. McClintock taught the first school.

The first piling bridge in this county was built in that year by A. D. Griffin and T. S. McElhaney. The piles were cut from the homestead of Mr. McElhaney.

In the nineties there were in operation in Le Mars numerous factories, including a shoe factory, the Gould Manufacturing Company, making mill machinery and the Harpe Clothing Manufacturing Company, makers of ready-made clothing.

A WHOLESALE GROCERY HOUSE.

The Laux & Wernli wholesale grocery house of Le Mars was established in the fall of 1892, at the corner of Seventh and Main streets, with a large warehouse in another part of the city. The first invoice consisted of many carloads of groceries. A thriving business was carried on for many years, but finally the many larger wholesale houses at near-by Sioux City, with other causes, ended the business.

AN EARLY DIRECTORY.

According to the _Sentinel_ files of 1871 the railroad time-table showed that passenger trains going west stopped at Le Mars station for dinners at the depot hotel.

The Le Mars Cemetery Association was organized with John Blodget as president; A. P. Gilbert, secretary; J. W. Young, treasurer; B. F. Betsworth and S. Reeves, directors.

This early file also shows that it had not been long before mail was received from Cherokee and Sioux City once each week, but at that date it came daily from Sioux City, as parties there forwarded the mail, the patrons here paying the Sioux City hotel keeper for taking the mail sack from the postoffice to the depot in that city. The Cherokee people “beefed” because they had to pay individuals at Sioux City to Deliver mail at the train for them.

“Gordon's Corner” seems to have been the commercial center of the village of Le Mars in 1871-2. Gordon's store stood where the Wasmer steam laundry now stands – opposite the Grand Central Hotel of today. A. M. Duus was then clerking for Gordon. An editorial in Vol. I., No. 1, of the _Sentinel,_ in reviewing the conditions in Europe, where food and work were very scarce for the poorer classes, took occasion to say: “Come to America. Here in Plymouth county, a small fragment of the state of Iowa, we have room for many more; land can be purchased at from three to ten dollars an acre, and if you cannot pay that, we have Lyon and Sioux counties at the north where the government will give you a tract of one hundred and sixty acres for nothing.” (Homestead land.) That paper reached England and after a time it returned like bread cast upon the waters. Many English came – some with plenty of money and others with little, but all made good by immigrating to Plymouth county. Le Mars was a for a number of years known as “the English town.” The English settlers built “the House of Lords,” an English hotel and resort, and brought to this county many games and sports such as polo and the like, besides purchasing many thousands of acres of land in Garfield and other townships, all of which they improved and tilled for many years, being aided materially by the Yankee farmers.

The greatest industry Le Mars has ever enjoyed is her mammoth flour-mill enterprise, the climax of which industry is the present Plymouth roller mills. From the earliest day, this city and the surrounding country has been blessed with excellent flour-making mills.

The first mill at Le Mars was the one situated in the north part of the town, on the banks of the Floyd river, which stream furnished the motive power by which the mill was operated. It was built and owned by Peter Gehlen, who visited this vicinity in 1869 and concluded to utilize the water power of the Floyd for milling purposes, by throwing a dam across the stream at this point. This pioneer mill was put in successful operation in 1870. It was a mill of the old style buhr-stone process, four runs of stones being employed. The Floyd river then afforded a nine-foot “head” of water, which was utilized by two James Leffell turbine waterwheels. In 1873 steam power was added and was thereafter used in conjunction with the power derived from the waters of the uncertain Floyd. In 1885 this mill was overhauled and thoroughly remodeled, and the new process of flour making was installed. Rolls were put in and all up-to-date appliances, as then known, supplemented the original, old-style machinery. When remodeled the mill had a capacity of seventy-five barrels of flour daily, besides which the daily output of feed was five carloads. In all, this mill had fourteen sets of rolls – making the “patent process” flour. In 1889 an elevator holding thirty thousand bushels of grain was erected and in 1890 the “Omaha” road provided a side-track to the mill and elevator. This mill used to ship both flour and feed as far away as the northern pineries of Wisconsin, and the mining towns of the far West, Wyoming, Montana, Colorado and beyond. The founder of these mills died in the eighties and his sons and S. J. Herron operated the plant successfully for many years thereafter. Later the company became involved and by virtue of claims held by the First National Bank the property was turned over to that bank and a few years ago it was torn down. The grounds in that portion of the city have since become a beautiful and valuable residence section of the city, the Daltons and others having made the place a real beauty spot. The old mill remains only in the memory of the people who lived here years ago.

THE PLYMOUTH ROLLER MILLS.   
The Plymouth roller mills – one of Iowa's largest flour-making plants – has, in many ways, had a very interesting andd eventful history, with all the success that has crowned its operation. Once it went down in flame, but Phoenix-like, rose from its ashes to become greater than before.

In 1876 Frank and Fred Burns moved a milling plant from Aurora, Illinois, and set it up in Le Mars, in the midst of what was hen a great wheat-growing belt. The mill at that time consisted of eight runs of buhrs. Not possessing sufficient capital themselves to carry on a very extensive business, the proprietors formed a stock company and were then able to make many needed improvements and to more successfully conduct a modern milling business, for a number of years the firm being known as Burns, Treat Company. At eleven o'clock at night, June 22, 1884 “fire-bugs” set this mill on fire and totally consumed it with all its contents, causing a loss of ninety-five thousand dollars, with only thirty thousand dollars of insurance. Le Mars was at that date the home of several lawless and unworthy citizens, a few of whom got into political rings and for a time seemed to run things to suit themselves. No convictions were ever made for the burning of the mill.

At the time the property was burned it was owned by P. F. Dalton, A. H. Treat, Frank and Fred Burns and J. H. Freeman, good business men, who had an abiding faith in the milling industry for Le Mars and Plymouth county. They set to work and furnished capital to reorganize the business, and on August 16, following the burning of the mill, the old firm merged into what was styled “The Plymouth Roller Mill Company.” Its president was P. F. Dalton, who was also the treasurer; A. H. Treat, vice-president; Frank W. Burns, superintendent; W. J. Wernli, secretary. The work of rebuilding was begun on September 1, 1884, and on January 12, 1885, four months later, the new mill was ready for the production of flour, from an enlarged plant, with greater capacity, greater facilities in every way and a good set of buildings. The structure consisted of a corrugated-iron building of large proportions and four stories high. Its construction, with that of the adjacent grain elevator, required thirty-three carloads of lumber, and thirty-five thousand pounds of nails. Its cost was one hundred thousand dollars and its daily capacity of flour was three hundred barrels.

Of this milling plant a former history, published in 1889, said: “This is the largest single mill in Iowa, and in addition to the flour-making capacity of three hundred barrels daily, it also turns out twelve carloads of twenty-eight thousand pounds each, of feed, which is sent to distant points throughout the Northwest. The business of the mill is one-half million dollars annually. The thirty-eight sets of rolls are propelled by a 250-horse-power engine. Fuel for running this costss only one dollar and fifty cents a ton. An immense grain elevator of 250,000 bushels capacity was built in 1886."

These mills have several times been enlarged and improved to keep pace with the wonderful improvements in the production of mill products. They now employ from fifty to sixty men; expend eighty thousand dollars a year, of which one-half is paid out as salaries. Eight thousand tons of coal are annually consumed for running the machinery by steam power; sixty barrels of lubricating oils are used in a single year. Corn products from this plant go forth to all parts off the world, especially to the West Indies. Flour goes to England, Ireland, Scotland and the Netherlands. The capacity of the mills at present is about fourteen hundred barrels daily.

The officers of the company are: Fred W. Burns, president; E. A. Dalton, treasurer, and C. A. Wernli, secretary.

WATERWORKS AND ELECTRIC-LIGHT PLANT.

The Le Mars waterworks was established by J. M. Dunn and later was acquired by J. H. Winchel, in 1888. The electric-light plant was established in connection with the same in 1891, gas having been employed prior to that date. These combined plants cost not far from one hundred and forty thousand dollars. The water was obtained from a stratum of thirty feet of clean gravel and sand and two Holly direct-pressure pumps forced two million gallons of water daily through the mains of the city. The quality of water is almost absolutely pure – like a distilled water. inn 1893 there were twenty-one miles of water pipes within the city. The water-works changed hands in July, 1898, being taken over by the German State Bank, of Le Mars, on a debt. A new corporation was formed and John Winchel was placed in charge again as superintendent. There had been a reorganized company formed in 1893, along with the establishment of the lighting plant. The capital of the company was then raised to two hundred thousand dollars, and the officers were: J. H. Winchel, president; Dr. M. W. Richey, vice-president; J. K. Alline, secretary and treasurer.

The vote giving a franchise to the electric-light department of the plant in 1891, under John Winchel, stood three hundred and fifty for and fifty-two against the proposition. It was not long before there was a three-hundred-horse-power engine working; three dynamos in operation and more than forty miles of wire strung in the city. The plant is now private property and is operated by the Le Mars Water and Light Company.

Ever since 1884 the city of Le Mars has had the benefit of artificial gas for illuminating and heating purposes. It was in 1883 that J. H. ### . . . about Akron, Iowa

_From a 1917 History._

**THE TOWN OF AKRON.**

The incorporated town of Akron, on the line of the Sioux City division of the Chicago, St. Paul & Milwaukee Railroad, was originally platted as "Portlandville," by Sargent & Crill, in 1871. It is located handsomely in section 31, its plat extending to the Big Sioux river on the west. The river there affords a splendid water power, which has been utilized for many years.

The commencement of business at Akron (old Portlandville) was in 1871, when E. W. Sargent opened a general-merchandising store, soon followed by Martin & Dorsey. Mr. Sargent handled the first grain there, both as a milling man and a shipper by rail. The first to sell lumber was S. Bevins and the first live-stock man was Thomas Sedgewick. The pioneer blacksmith was M. W. Toppings; Henry L. Waterbury was the first harnessmaker. The first retail merchant was J. Booth. The first hardware merchant was William Love, in 1877. The first to engage in the drug trade was L. H. Farmer. The earliest implement dealer was M. L. Disbrow. The first to handle furniture was August Peterson. The main street of the village was named after the landlord of the first boarding house and two other streets, Sargent and Hardy, perpetuate the names of the early residents.

The first child born in Portlandville was a son of Mr. and Mrs. George Reed, in August, 1871, the second being a son of Mr. and Mrs. H. D. Barr in the spring of 1872.

The first school was taught by Mrs. E. B. Donaldson in 1873 at her home, and the same year a school house was built at a cost of three thousand dollars.

**SPLENDID LOCATION FOR WATER-POWER.**

The land on which was located the original village of Portlandville, now Akron, was homesteaded by Thomas and John McLain in 1857. There were no permanent settlers on the land for a decade or more after this date and the tract changed hands a number of times before 1871. For several years previous to this date E. W. Sargent and L. N. Crill had been operating the "Big Sioux" flour and saw-mill, about fifteen miles down the river. In the spring of 1871 these gentlemen desired to extend their business by establishing a flour-mill farther up the river and finally decided that the comparatively high banks of the river at the point now called Akron afforded a splendid location for a water-power. Accordingly they bought, at the munificent price of five dollars an acre, the tract of land surrounding that point and prepared to dam the river, build a mill and lay out a townsite. There were at that time no settlers in what is now Portland township, with the single exception of J. B. Hughes, who had located on the land immediately east of that bought by Sargent and Crill and was living there until he could "prove up," which he did in the fall of 1872.

When the construction of the new mill was decided upon, Sargent and Crill prepared the lumber for it at their plant and hauled the material by teams to the proper place. H. D. Barr hauled in the lumber for the first building in the new settlement, a small shanty owned by a man named Readan and located at what is now the corner of First and Dakota streets. Following this were erected a hotel constructed of rough boards, and a dwelling for H. D. Barr. The hotel, or boarding house, was owned by George Reed and was located on the present site of the Opera House block. About that time was built, south of the mill, a small store, operated by E. W. Sargent.

In the year that the railroad reached Portlandville, which was in 1876, Mr. Sargent built the first grain elevator on the north side of Reed street. During that same year the _Portlandville Blade_ was launched by James W. Sheppard.

**POSTOFFICE HISTORY.**

During the first two years of the history of this village, mail was brought weekly by a one-horse rig, which followed the river from Sioux City to Sioux Falls. In 1873 was established the first regular post office, mail being brought from Elk Point. T. S. Martin was the first postmaster and his successors were as follow: C. E. Robinson, Amy Hampton, F. T. Sheppard, 1Ir. Peck, B. B. Harrington, A. L. McGinnis, C. P. Kilbourn, B. F. Winterstein, H. J. Muhs, Mrs. M. A. Muhs and Bezie Dee. Several rural routes radiate from this post office. There are now three going into South Dakota and four altogether in Iowa. At first this was known as Portlandville post office, but on account of there being found another town by this long name in Iowa, it was changed to Akron, in 1882. A money-order station was established there on July 1, 1878, and the first order was issued to David Strohben, for the sum of thirty dollars, payable at Traer, Iowa.

**MUNICIPAL HISTORY.**

The census of 1880 showed that the village had a population of two hundred and forty-two. Two years later came the agitation for separate town government. The petition for incorporation, signed by thirty voters, stated that the village had a population of three hundred. At an election held on September 7, 1882, incorporation was decided upon by a vote of forty-one to sixteen. The new town was christened Akron, a name selected by Mr. Sargent, as the old name was considered too long. The first officers included the following: James Biddlecome, mayor; A. P. Douglas, clerk; H. J. Muhs, treasurer; R. D. Clark, assessor; A. H. Smith, marshal; E. W. Sargent, L. H. Farnham, B. B. Harrington, R. E. Blades and J. Beaulieu, councilmen. The following men have served as mayor: James Biddlecome, E. H. Tryon, A. L. McGinnis, S. G. Baker, M. A. Agnes, J. P. Kendall, A. G. A. Palm, O. F. Haskell, W. C. Bryant, Tim Sullivan, William Slaughter, R. A. Smith, Dr. G. H. Wooten, N. S. Moore, and A. L. Yeaton, the present incumbent.

The town officers of 1916 include the following: A. L. Yeaton, mayor; F. W. Burnett, clerk; J. L. Beck, treasurer; J. H. Kerr, health physician; C. P. Vargason, marshal; J. C. Rogers, superintendent of light and water plant; R. A. Broadbent, J. B. Klauer, E. H. Youngstrom, Ernest Ostrom, H. Shoulberg and T. L. Burnight, councilmen.

**SCHOOLS AND PUBLIC UTILITIES.**

In 1882 was built the present school building, at a cost of ten thousand dollars. After a few years an addition was necessary and two rooms were added on the north side. In 1907 a new addition, thirty by fifty feet, was constructed, at a cost of six thousand dollars. At the present time with an enrollment of three hundred and twenty-five the building is overcrowded and a room formerly used by the Commercial Club is used for school purposes. Prof. A. Huffman is superintendent of the school and eleven teachers are employed. Eighty pupils are enrolled in the high school, the largest number in the history of the school.

Among the public utilities of the town is an excellent waterworks system, with mains and laterals throughout the city, and up on the hill, on the east side, is the reservoir of eighty thousand gallons. The electric light plant has recently been taken over by the municipality and gives the town day and night service. For a period of five years the Akron Milling Company furnished the town with electricity and at the end of that period the municipality assumed control.

The streets of the town are wide, handsome and well shaded, and many miles of cement sidewalks have been laid during the last few years, supplanting the old board walks. During the summer of 1916 seven blocks of cement streets were laid in the business district of the town at a cost of twenty thousand dollars. In the town are an unusual number of substantial business houses and modern residences, surrounded by well-kept lawns filled with flowers, shrubbery, fruit and shade trees.

**ATTRACTIVE RECREATION POINTS.**

Among the attractive features are the numerous picnic grounds and shady nooks along the Big Sioux river near the town, furnishing respite from the heat and dust of the summer, and where one may enjoy a day's outing beneath the cooling shades and fish from the banks of the river.

At one time the town of Akron possessed one of the most active Conmmercial Clubs of any municipality in the county. The club, organized on March 2, 1909, began its work under the most auspicious circumstances. The first officers included H. W. Fields, president; G. H. Wooton and C. G. Brady, vice-presidents; W. W. Burrill, secretary; F. J. Swanson, treasurer. Club rooms were fitted up and the spirit of the organization was of the very best. Many questions of civic and municipal interest were discussed and decided upon and the good accomplished was far-reaching. With some of the more important questions settled for all time, the importance of the club was somewhat lessened, with the result that it has gradually fallen into a dormant state.

The worst fire in Akron's history occurred in April, 1905, causing a loss of fifty thousand dollars. The building burned was the fine two-story business block known as the Clark-Cilley-Baker building, a brick and stone structure.

**THE AKRON MILL.**

Akron's first milling plant was erected in the year 1871 by E. W. Sargent, being one of the first mills in this section of the Northwest. The concern changed hands so many times that it is difficult to name the various owners, but at the time of its destruction by fire in 1898, Messrs. Fields, Slaughter & Miller were the proprietors.

Before the embers of the old mill, had ceased smoking and in the face of the heavy loss, the management was planning upon the erection of a much larger mill to be equipped with all of the latest machinery. Within one day less than five months from the date of the old mill's destruction, the new mill ground the first grist. The maximum capacity of the plant during twenty-four hours is one hundred and twenty-five barrels of flour and forty tons of feed, besides other products such as corn meal and graham flour.

The mill was rebuilt at a cost of ten thousand dollars and at present is owned by a corporation known as the Akron Milling Company.

**BUSINESS FACTORS IN 1916.**

The business and professional interests of Akron in the autumn of 1916 were represented by the following:

- Auto garages - Wade & Burnight, E. Ostrom, F. C. Olson, Henry Callaghan.   
 - Attorneys - W.T. Kidd, Yeaton & Ross.   
 - Auctioneers - J. J. Aalfs, W. H. Morse, F. C. Olson.   
 - Banks - The First National Bank, The Akron Savings Bank.   
 - Barbers - F. J. Montague, Hilzemann Bros., Trautt Brothers.   
 - Blacksmiths - C. M. Hilliker & Son, Robert Schmidt, H. Bohlen.   
 - Bottling works - Akron Ice Cream and Bottling Works.   
 - Bakery - William Simeon.   
 - Clothing and furnishings Burrill - Douglas Company.   
 - Confectionery - William Eberle, William Simeon.   
 - Cement block works - C. M. Hilliker & Son.   
 - Dray line - A. C. Jenkins, Charles Wise, ______ Chamberlain.   
 - Dentists - Dr. D. J. Conger, Dr. George Wooten.   
 - Elevators - Farmers Elevator Company, Hunting Elevator, J. W. Hedges.   
 - Furniture dealers - Klauser-Swanson Co., J. B. Cunningham.   
 - Feed mill - Akron Milling Company.   
 - Feed barns - Bohlen Bros., F. Twormbley.   
 - Grocery and meat market - Harry Cohen.   
 - General merchants - O. M. Silkebakken, Henry Rohrer, Paul Wendt, George Dudley.   
 - Hotels - The New Kendall, The Nall Hotel.   
 - Harness - A. Metz, F. Smythe.   
 - Hardware - Klauer-Swanson Company, J. B. Cunningham.   
 - Implements - W. W. Keach, VonHagel & Koch, Akron Implement Company.   
 - Ice dealers - Cross & Dilly, August Kruger.   
 - Jewelers - William E. Whitney, Benjamin Winterstein.

 - Merchant tailors - Earl & Walrod, A. E. Lipp.

 - Opera house - Akron Opera House.   
 - Physicians - Dr. W. J. Bruner, Dr. J. H. Kerr, Dr. George Mattison.

### . . . about Brunsville, Iowa

_From a 1917 History._

**VILLAGE OF BRUNSVILLE.**

When the townsite of Brunsville was laid out by the Western Townsite Company, there was a need of a general market and a trading center in the community and after due deliberation the land owned by Mrs. Brun was chosen, and the village was named in her honor. An eighty-acre tract was platted and within a few months a cow pasture was transformed into a thriving village. Edward Johnson was the first man to see the opportunities of the place in a business way and he established the first general store. Others soon followed and as will be noticed by the present business directory, most of the staple lines of business are represented:   
 * Banks - Bank of Brunsville, Farmers Bank.   
 * Blacksmiths - Fred Toel, George Benton.   
 * Creamery - Plymouth Creamery Company, Jobe Kennedy, manager.   
 * Elevators - Farmers Elevator Company, Frank Hoese.   
 * General dealers - Edward Johnson, John Hauschildt.   
 * Hardware and harness - John F. Dirks.   
 * Implements - George E. Pew.   
 * Lumber dealer - Brunsville Lumber Company, George Popken, manager.   
 * Meat market - Nate Gearke.   
 * Physician - Dr. C. G. Ellsworth.   
 * Restaurant - C. M. Richards.

During the spring of 1911 the citizens of the village cherished a desire to become a distinct municipality and articles of incorporation were secured. The first municipal election resulted in the election of the following: C. M. Richards, mayor; Ed Johnson, treasurer; B. J. Luken, Clerk; J. H. Dirks, B. H. Luken, O. F. Vollmar, Fred Toel, councilmen. The present officers include the following: O. E. Pecks, mayor; Jobe Kennedy, clerk; Edward Johnson, treasurer; Henry Johnson, Fred Toel, T. M. Harms, J. W. Hauschildt and George Popken, councilmen. Although the village is yet in its infancy, it has shown great strides in business and civic improvement. Several blocks of cement walks have been laid and many new and modern dxellings have been erected with an idea of permanency. The business houses are modern and substantial, a fact that goes to show the confidence the people have in the future of the town.

_[History of Plymouth County, Iowa, W. S. Freeman, Editor, published by B.F. Bowen & Co., Indianapolis, 1917. Submitted by Mary Kay Krogman.]_

### . . . about Hinton, Iowa

_From a 1917 History._

**THE VILLAGE OF HINTON.**

Hinton, a station point of the various railroads passing through there, is situated in section 8 of Hungerford township. The post office was established there in 1883, with Samuel Davis as postmaster. He was succeeded by H. S. Hubbard, B. F. Bogenrief, G. W. Sheets, M. H. Mammen, and the present postmaster, Mr. Winter. The first hotel was conducted by Mrs. H. E. Winters.

**VARIOUS INTERESTS IN 1916.**

In the autumn of 1916 the interests of Hinton were summed up as follow:

- Auto garage - O. C. Brown & Son, William Schneider.   
 - Banks - Bank of Hinton, Security Bank.   
 - Barber - J. H. Levins.   
 - Blacksmith - Herbert G. Soule.   
 - Druggist - P. S. Tronsrue.   
 - Elevators - Atlas Elevator Company, Thorpe Elevator Company, Farmers Co-Operative.   
 - General dealers - E. M. Winter, Reliable Mercantile Company.   
 - Hardware dealer - Haas-Thuenk Hardware Company.   
 - Hotel - Hinto Hotel.   
 - Implements - Hauff Brothers.   
 - Lumber - S. H. Bowman Company, Farmers Co-Operative Company.   
 - Meat market - A. J. Taylor.   
 - Newspaper - The Hinton Gazette.   
 - Physician - Dr. J. H. Robbins.   
 - Restaurants - Hawkeye Cafe, Mrs. B. Kay.   
 - Real-estate dealer - Westmore Land Company.

The village of Hinton, although small, exerts quite a good deal of influence locally. It is situated in the heart of an excellent agricultural community and the volume of trade transacted at this point is larger than that of many towns many times its size. The village has excellent schools and churches, which are a true index of the character of the people. The school building, which was built in 1906, is quite overcrowded and a movement for a new consolidated school building is on foot. Six teachers are employed and H. H. Foster is principal. The enrollment is one hundred and thirty.

Hinton was incorporated about 1907, but the records are not to be found today. The 1916 officers are: John Casper, mayor; George Ellison, clerk; H. C. Brown, treasurer; J. H. Thompson, J. I. Levins, H. J. Schneider, T. S. Tronsrue and H. G. Soule, councilmen.

On May 23, 1914, Hinton was visited, at half past one o'clock in the morning, by a fire that destroyed five buildings causing a loss of thirty thousand dollars. These buildings were the Bank of Hinton, H. F. Bogenrief & Son's hardware store, B. S. Tronsrue's drug store, H. H. Lever's barber shop, Crouche's restaurant, Doctor Robbin's office, the Hotel Hinton and the residence of E. M. Winter, partly destroyed. The fire originated in the hardware store. The buildings were all frame structures and were soon replaced by substantial brick buildings. The town had no fire protection whatever at the date of this fire.

_[History of Plymouth County, Iowa, W. S. Freeman, Editor, published by B.F. Bowen & Co., Indianapolis, 1917. Submitted by Mary Kay Krogman.]_

### . . . about Kingsley, Iowa

_From a 1917 History._

**THE TOWN OF KINGSLEY.**

The town of Kingsley became an incorporated town in 1884. The place was platted in section 32 of Garfield township on June 4, 1883, following the building of the Chicago & Northwestern railroad through from the east to Moville, later extending on to Sioux City. Kingsley is the next largest town in the county to Le Mars, the seat of justice. In 1890 it had a population of 649; in 1900 it had reached 720, and in 1910 the United States census gave it as having a population of 977. It is a busy up-to-date town supported by a wonderfully rich, well-developed agricultural section. From its earliest inception this place has been noted for the business snap and genuine enterprise of its business factors. As early as 1890 there were over sixty business houses, including two excellent banks and a live local newspaper, which are mentioned at length in chapters on these topics. The town is beautifully situated on high, rolling ground, and has broad well-kept streets. The first attempt at opening business there was in the summer of 1883, following the completion of the railroad. An old village, known as Quorn, was platted in 1880 by the Close brothers, with whom the railroad had a misunderstanding, which resulted in a change of plan on the part of the company, which changed its original route and located what is now Kingsley. The few dealers at Quorn soon removed their business to the railroad town, which was only a mile to the west.

THE BEGINNINGS OF THINGS AT KINGSLEY.   
The first persons to embark in business at Kingsley were Gasper Brothers, with a general-merchandise store. This firm removed from Quorn in August, 1883. J. F. Varner, another pioneer in Quorn, moved his stock of goods to Kingsley about the date last mentioned. The first house erected was built for saloon purposes. The Curtis House, built by John Curtis, was the first hotel in the town. The first hardware was sold by Rathbun & Ireland, who removed from Quorn. The first to engage in the sale of agricultural implements were Rathbun & Ireland. The earliest lumber dealers were Lewis & Brockman. The pioneer grain dealers were Herron Brothers, who continued many years; they also handled large amounts of live stock, buying and shipping. C. H. Loring was the first to engage in the furniture trade. The village blacksmith was Charles Bowers. The first wagon shop was conducted by M. A. Oberholser. The harness business was first repreresented by that master leather-worker, M. A. Condon, who later moved to Le Mars and there carried on a large shop. The drug business was first repreresented in Kingsley by Marshall & Banks. Scott Brothers sold the first meat from a small butcher shop. Hamil Brothers was the first firm to conduct a general livery business and later Trotter Brothers had an up-to-date stable.

EVIDENCES OF PROGRESSIVE METHODS.   
Kingsley, is one of the most prosperous towns in Plymouth county, well as as in the Northwest, and, according to the last census, made the greatest growth of any town in the county during the ten years previous. The town shows the imprint of prosperous business men who are ever alert to make Kingsley a greater and better town. The town's population represents several nationalities and at the present time numbers about one thousand.

The neat and commodious churches, with their spires pointing heavenward, are indications of the character of the citizens. Almost all religious denominations are represented and are well supplied with comfortable houses in which to worship. The Methodist church was the first to perfect an organization in the village, but other denominations soon followed and they are all united in an aggressive and uncompromising warfare against sin in whatever form or name it may be found.

The school history of the town is indeed interesting. Soon after the town was platted a school was necessary, on account of the rapid growth of the village. During the first year school was held in empty buildings about the town. The following year, 1885, a school building consisting of four rooms and a recitation room was constructed and was used until 1894, when a two-room addition was made. This served the needs of the town and community until 1912 when a new building became an absolute necessity.

One of the most important events in the history of Kingsley occurred on October 27, 1912, the date of the laying of the cornerstone of the new thirty-thousand-dollar school building. Much interest was manifested in the affairs and it was an occasion of great rejoicing by both old and young. While the weather was bad and many were thus kept away, yet the services were attended by more than one thousand people. The Masonic order of Kingsley had charge of the services and Rabbi Joseph Raush, of Sioux City delivered the address. The building is of brick and stone and contains sixteen rooms, including a fine gymnasium. The site is one of the very best in the state and the building one of the most completely equipped. The present enrollment numbers about three hundred.

_[History of Plymouth County, Iowa, W. S. Freeman, Editor, published by B.F. Bowen & Co., Indianapolis, 1917. Submitted by Mary Kay Krogman.]_
