A royal charter from King Charles II incorporated "The Governor and Company of Adventurers of England, trading into Hudson's Bay" on 2 May 1670.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-charter-23) The charter granted the company a monopoly over the region drained by all rivers and streams flowing into Hudson Bay in northern parts of present-day Canada, taking part on behalf of England. The area was named "[Rupert's Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupert's_Land "Rupert's Land")"[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-24) after Prince Rupert,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-25) the first governor of the company appointed by the King. This drainage basin of Hudson Bay spans 3,861,400 square kilometres (1,490,900 sq mi),[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-26) comprising over one-third of the area of modern-day Canada, and stretches into the present-day north-central [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). The specific boundaries remained unknown at the time. Rupert's Land would eventually become Canada's largest land ["purchase"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Rupert's_Land_and_North-Western_Territory_transfer "Timeline of Rupert's Land and North-Western Territory transfer") in the 19th century.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-27)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Charter_of_the_Hudsons_Bay_Company.jpg/250px-Charter_of_the_Hudsons_Bay_Company.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Charter_of_the_Hudsons_Bay_Company.jpg)

Charter of the HBC

The HBC established six posts between 1668 and 1717. Rupert House (1668, southeast),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVoorhis1930152-28)[Moose Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moose_Factory "Moose Factory") (1673, south)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVoorhis1930119-29) and [Fort Albany, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Albany,_Ontario "Fort Albany, Ontario") (1679, west)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVoorhis193030-30) were erected on James Bay; three other posts were established on the western shore of Hudson Bay proper: [New Severn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Severn "New Severn") (1685),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-31)[York Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Factory "York Factory") (1684), and [Fort Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Churchill,_Manitoba "Churchill, Manitoba") (1717). Inland posts [were not built](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asleep_by_the_frozen_sea "Asleep by the frozen sea") until 1774. After 1774, York Factory became the main post because of its convenient access to the vast interior waterway-systems of the [Saskatchewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan_River "Saskatchewan River") and [Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_of_the_North "Red River of the North") rivers. Originally called "factories" because the ["factor"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factor_(agent) "Factor (agent)"), i.e., a person acting as a mercantile agent, did business from there, these posts operated in the manner of the Dutch fur-trading operations in [New Netherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Netherland "New Netherland"). By adoption of the Standard of Trade in the 18th century, the HBC ensured consistent pricing throughout Rupert's Land. A means of exchange arose based on the "[Made Beaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Made_Beaver "Made Beaver")" (MB); a prime pelt, worn for a year and ready for processing: "the prices of all trade goods were set in values of Made Beaver (MB) with other animal pelts, such as squirrel, otter and moose quoted in their MB (made beaver) equivalents. For example, two otter pelts might equal 1 MB".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-32)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Indians_at_a_Hudson_Bay_Company_trading_post.jpg/250px-Indians_at_a_Hudson_Bay_Company_trading_post.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Indians_at_a_Hudson_Bay_Company_trading_post.jpg)

Trading at an HBC trading post

During the fall and winter, [First Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Nations_in_Canada "First Nations in Canada") men and European [fur trappers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_trapping "Fur trapping") accomplished the vast majority of the animal trapping and pelt preparation. They travelled by [canoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canoe "Canoe") and on foot to the forts to sell their pelts. In exchange they typically received popular trade-goods such as knives, kettles, beads, needles, and the [Hudson's Bay point blanket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_point_blanket "Hudson's Bay point blanket"). The arrival of the First Nations trappers was one of the high points of the year, met with pomp and circumstance. The highlight was very formal, an almost ritualized "trading ceremony" between the chief trader and the captain of the Indigenous contingent who traded on their behalf.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-33) During the initial years of the fur trade, prices for items varied from post to post.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-34)

The early coastal factory model of the English contrasted with the system of the French, who established an extensive system of inland posts at native villages and sent traders to live among the tribes of the region, learning their languages and often forming alliances through marriages with Indigenous women. In March 1686 the French sent a [raiding party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay_expedition_(1686) "Hudson Bay expedition (1686)") under the [Chevalier de Troyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_de_Troyes,_Chevalier_de_Troyes "Pierre de Troyes, Chevalier de Troyes") more than 1,300 km (810 mi) to capture the HBC posts along James Bay. The French appointed [Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Le_Moyne_d'Iberville "Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville"), who had shown great heroism during the raids, as commander of the company's captured posts. In 1687 an English attempt to [resettle Fort Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Albany "Battle of Fort Albany") failed due to strategic deceptions by d'Iberville. After 1688 England and France [were officially at war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_William's_War "King William's War"), and the conflict played out in North America as well. D'Iberville raided Fort Severn in 1690 but did not attempt to raid the well-defended local headquarters at York Factory. In 1693 the HBC [recovered Fort Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Albany_(1693) "Battle of Fort Albany (1693)"); d'Iberville [captured York Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_York_Factory "Capture of York Factory") in 1694, but the company recovered it the next year.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewman1986151%E2%80%93158-35)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/La_prise_fort_Bourbon_dans_la_baie_d%27Hudson_en_1694_par_les_Fran%C3%A7ais.jpg/250px-La_prise_fort_Bourbon_dans_la_baie_d%27Hudson_en_1694_par_les_Fran%C3%A7ais.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:La_prise_fort_Bourbon_dans_la_baie_d'Hudson_en_1694_par_les_Fran%C3%A7ais.jpg)

Depiction of the [capture of York Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_York_Factory "Capture of York Factory") by French forces in 1694

In 1697, d'Iberville again commanded a French naval raid on York Factory. On the way to the fort he defeated three ships of the Royal Navy in the [Battle of Hudson's Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hudson's_Bay "Battle of Hudson's Bay") (5 September 1697), the largest naval battle in the history of the North American Arctic. D'Iberville's depleted French force captured York Factory by laying siege to the fort and pretending to be a much larger army. The French retained all of the outposts except Fort Albany until 1713. A small French and Indian force attacked Fort Albany again [in 1709](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Albany_(1709) "Battle of Fort Albany (1709)") during [Queen Anne's War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Anne's_War "Queen Anne's War") but was unsuccessful. The economic consequences of the French possession of these posts for the company were significant; the HBC did not pay any dividends for more than 20 years. See [Anglo-French conflicts on Hudson Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-French_conflicts_on_Hudson_Bay "Anglo-French conflicts on Hudson Bay").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewman1986160%E2%80%93164-36)

## 18th-century history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 18th-century history")]

With the ending of the [Nine Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Years'_War "Nine Years' War") in 1697, and the [War of the Spanish Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Spanish_Succession "War of the Spanish Succession") in 1713 with the signing of the [Treaty of Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Utrecht "Treaty of Utrecht"), France had made substantial concessions. Among the treaty's many provisions, it required France to relinquish all claims to Great Britain on the Hudson Bay, which again became a British possession.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewman1985352-37) (The [Kingdom of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain "Kingdom of Great Britain") had been established following the union of Scotland and England in 1707).

After the treaty, the HBC built [Prince of Wales Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Wales_Fort "Prince of Wales Fort"), a stone [star fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_fort "Star fort") at the mouth of the nearby [Churchill River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Churchill_River_(Hudson_Bay) "Churchill River (Hudson Bay)").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewman1986202%E2%80%93206-38) In 1782, during the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_operations_in_the_American_Revolutionary_War "Naval operations in the American Revolutionary War"), a French squadron under [Jean-François de Galaup, comte de Lapérouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Fran%C3%A7ois_de_Galaup,_comte_de_Lap%C3%A9rouse "Jean-François de Galaup, comte de Lapérouse")[captured and demolished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay_expedition "Hudson Bay expedition") York Factory and Prince of Wales Fort in support of the American rebels.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewman1986366%E2%80%93371-39)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/A_Canadian_Squaw.jpg/250px-A_Canadian_Squaw.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_Canadian_Squaw.jpg)

Depiction of an Indigenous woman wearing a [Hudson's Bay point blanket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_point_blanket "Hudson's Bay point blanket"), c.1850

In its trade with Indigenous peoples, Hudson's Bay Company exchanged wool blankets, called Hudson's Bay point blankets, for the beaver pelts trapped by Indigenous hunters. By 1700, point blankets accounted for more than 60 per cent of the trade.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-40) The number of [indigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigo "Indigo") stripes (a.k.a. points) woven into the blankets identified its finished size. A long-held misconception is that the number of stripes was related to its value in beaver pelts.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-41)

A parallel may be drawn between the HBC's control over Rupert's Land with the trade monopoly and government functions enjoyed by the [East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company "East India Company") over India during roughly the same period. The HBC invested £10,000 in the East India Company in 1732, which it viewed as a major competitor.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTERich195838,_42,_491-42)

Hudson's Bay Company's first inland trading post was established by [Samuel Hearne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Hearne "Samuel Hearne") in 1774 with [Cumberland House, Saskatchewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_House,_Saskatchewan "Cumberland House, Saskatchewan").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-DNB_Hearne-43)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Hearne-44)

Conversely, a number of inland HBC "houses" pre-date the construction of Cumberland House, in 1774. Henley House, (HH) established in 1743, inland from Hudson Bay, at the confluence of the [Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany_River "Albany River") and Kenogami Rivers, a prime strategic location between Upland and Lowland Indigenous peoples, as well as the rival English and French traders. HH was dependent on Albany River – Fort Albany for lines of communication. Henley House was sacked in 1754, and its servants killed. Three of the five attackers (rebels?) were apprehended at Albany Fort and hanged on June 21, 1755. HH was raised a few years later, then rebuilt in 1759, only to be sacked again immediately.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-45) Next, the inland houses of Split Lake and Nelson Houses were established between 1740 and 1760. These were dependent on York River – York Factory and Churchill River, respectively. Although not inland, Richmond Fort was established in 1749. This was on an island within Hudson Bay. It was titled a "New Discovery" in 1749, and by 1750 was titled Richmond Gulf. The name was changed to Richmond Fort and given the abbreviation RF from 1756 to 1759, it served mainly as a trade goods and provisions storage location.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-46) Additional inland posts were Capusco River and Chickney Creek, both circa 1750. Likewise, Brunswick (1776), New Brunswick (1777), Gloucester (1777), Upper Hudson (ca. 1778), Lower Hudson (1779), Rupert, and Wapiscogami Houses were established in the 1770s.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-47)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-48)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-49)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-50)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-51) These post-date Cumberland House, yet speak to the expanding inland incursion of the HBC in the last quarter of the 18th century. Minor posts also during this time period include Mesackamy/Mesagami Lake (1777), Sturgeon Lake (1778), and Beaver Lake Posts.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-52)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-53)

On their way to Canada from London, the Company's ships would call in at [Stromness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stromness "Stromness") in [Orkney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkney "Orkney") to take on water and supplies. For most of the Eighteenth Century Orkney became the Company's principal recruiting ground. [[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-54)

In 1779, other traders founded the [North West Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_West_Company "North West Company") (NWC) in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal") as a seasonal partnership to provide more capital and to continue competing with the HBC. It became operative for the outfit of 1780 and was the first [joint-stock company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint-stock_company "Joint-stock company") in Canada and possibly North America. The agreement lasted one year. A second agreement established in 1780 had a three-year term. The company became a permanent entity in 1783.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewman1985354-55) By 1784, the NWC had begun to make serious inroads into the HBC's profits.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-56)

## 19th-century history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 19th-century history")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/The_Fight_at_Seven_Oaks.jpg/250px-The_Fight_at_Seven_Oaks.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Fight_at_Seven_Oaks.jpg)

Depiction of the [Battle of Seven Oaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Seven_Oaks "Battle of Seven Oaks"), a violent confrontation between HBC and the [North West Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_West_Company "North West Company") during the [Pemmican War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pemmican_War "Pemmican War")

The North West Company (NWC) was the main rival in the fur trade. The competition led to the small [Pemmican War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pemmican_War "Pemmican War") in 1816, which culminated in the [Battle of Seven Oaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Seven_Oaks "Battle of Seven Oaks") on 19 June 1816.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-57) In 1821, the NWC and Hudson's Bay Company were forcibly merged by intervention of the British government to put an end to the violent competition. Of the 175 posts, 68 of them the HBC's, were reduced to 52 for efficiency and because many were redundant as a result of the rivalry and were inherently unprofitable.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-58) Their combined territory was extended by a licence to the [North-Western Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North-Western_Territory "North-Western Territory"), which reached to the [Arctic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean "Arctic Ocean") in the north and, with the creation of the [Columbia Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Department "Columbia Department") in the [Pacific Northwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Northwest "Pacific Northwest"), to the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") in the west. The NWC's regional headquarters at [Fort George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Astoria "Fort Astoria") (Fort Astoria) was relocated to [Fort Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Vancouver "Fort Vancouver") by 1825, making it the HBC's base of operations on the [Pacific Slope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Slope "Pacific Slope").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewman1988369%E2%80%93370-59)

Before the merger, the employees of the HBC, unlike those of the NWC, did not participate in its profits. After the merger, with all operations under the management of [Sir George Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Simpson_(administrator) "George Simpson (administrator)") (1826–60), the company had a corps of commissioned officers: 25 chief factors and 28 chief traders, who shared in the company's profits during the monopoly years. Its trade covered 7,770,000 km 2 (3,000,000 sq mi), and it had 1,500 contract employees.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalbraith1957[httpsbooksgooglecombooksidfOscZfLNOQkCpgPA8_8%E2%80%9323]-60)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Hudsons_Bay_Company_currency_to_fur_traders_1820_Fort_York_%28crop%29.jpg/250px-Hudsons_Bay_Company_currency_to_fur_traders_1820_Fort_York_%28crop%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hudsons_Bay_Company_currency_to_fur_traders_1820_Fort_York_(crop).jpg)

Currency issued by the Hudson's Bay Company, 1820

Between 1820 and 1870, the HBC issued its own [paper money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banknote "Banknote"). The notes, denominated in sterling, were printed in London and issued at York Factory for circulation primarily in the [Red River Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_Colony "Red River Colony").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-61)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-62)

### Competition and exploration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Competition and exploration")]

Although the HBC maintained a monopoly on the fur trade during the early to mid-19th century, there was competition from James Sinclair and [Andrew McDermot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_McDermot "Andrew McDermot") (Dermott), independent traders in the Red River Colony. They shipped furs by the [Red River Trails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_Trails "Red River Trails") to [Norman Kittson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Kittson "Norman Kittson"),[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalbraith195760%E2%80%9372-63) a buyer in the United States. In addition, Americans controlled the [maritime fur trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_fur_trade "Maritime fur trade") on the Northwest Coast until the 1830s.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-64)

Throughout the 1820s and the 1830s, the HBC controlled nearly all trading operations in the Pacific Northwest region and was based at its headquarters at Fort Vancouver, on the [Columbia River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_River "Columbia River").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-65) Although claims to the region were by agreement in abeyance, commercial operating rights were nominally shared by the United States and Britain through the [Anglo-American Convention of 1818](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_1818 "Treaty of 1818"), but company policy, enforced via Chief Factor [John McLoughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLoughlin "John McLoughlin") of the company's [Columbia District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_District "Columbia District"), was to discourage US settlement of the territory. The company's effective monopoly on trade virtually forbade any settlement in the region.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewman1988370-66)

### Additional early presence in present-day United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Additional early presence in present-day United States")]

Over and above the NWC Fort George headquarters site, the HBC carried on the early presence in the region of the NWC when it merged in 1821 with noteworthy sites: [Spokane House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokane_House "Spokane House"), [Fort Okanogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Okanogan "Fort Okanogan") and [Fort Nez Percés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Nez_Perc%C3%A9s "Fort Nez Percés"). [Fort Colville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Colville "Fort Colville") located further North on the Columbia River replaced Spokane House in 1825.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-67)

In the mid-1820s, [Peter Skene Ogden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Skene_Ogden "Peter Skene Ogden") and a brigade of over 100 men pushed south to trap in the area that is now the state of [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah"). As one of the notable early European explorers in the region, several locations in northern Utah now bear Ogden's name, including the city of [Ogden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogden,_Utah "Ogden, Utah"),[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-68) the [Ogden Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogden_Valley,_Utah "Ogden Valley, Utah") and the [Ogden River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogden_River "Ogden River").

[Fort Umpqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Umpqua "Fort Umpqua") was established in 1832 in present-day southern [Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon "Oregon") after the [Willamette River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willamette_River "Willamette River") had been explored up toward its headwaters by mainly the NWC. Nisqually House was built during the same year to establish a presence further North on Puget Sound in present-day State of [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(State) "Washington (State)"), resulting in [Fort Nisqually](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Nisqually "Fort Nisqually") a few years later closer to present-day Canadian sites.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-69)

The HBC established [Fort Boise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Boise "Fort Boise") in 1834 (in present-day southwestern Idaho) to compete with the American [Fort Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Hall "Fort Hall"), 483 km (300 mi) to the east. In 1837, it purchased Fort Hall, also along the route of the [Oregon Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Trail "Oregon Trail"). The outpost director displayed the abandoned wagons of discouraged settlers to those seeking to move west along the trail.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMackie1998106%E2%80%93107-70)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Hudson%27s_Bay_Company_express_canoe.jpg/250px-Hudson%27s_Bay_Company_express_canoe.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hudson's_Bay_Company_express_canoe.jpg)

HBC officials in an express canoe crossing a lake, 1825

HBC trappers were also deeply involved in the early exploration and development of [Northern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_California "Northern California"). Company trapping brigades were sent south from Fort Vancouver, along what became known as the [Siskiyou Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siskiyou_Trail "Siskiyou Trail"), into Northern California as far south as the [San Francisco Bay Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay_Area "San Francisco Bay Area"), where the company operated a trading post at [Yerba Buena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yerba_Buena,_California "Yerba Buena, California") ([San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco")). The southern-most camp of the company was [French Camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Camp,_California#History "French Camp, California"), east of San Francisco in the Central Valley adjacent to the future site of the city of [Stockton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockton,_California "Stockton, California"). These trapping brigades in Northern California faced serious risks, and were often the first to explore relatively uncharted territory. They included the lesser known [Peter Skene Ogden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Skene_Ogden "Peter Skene Ogden") and [Samuel Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Black "Samuel Black").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-71)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-72)

The HBC also operated a store in what were then known as the Sandwich Islands (now the [Hawaiian Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Islands "Hawaiian Islands")), engaging in merchant shipping to the [island kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Kingdom "Hawaiian Kingdom") between 1828 and 1859.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-73)[Hawaiians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Hawaiians "Native Hawaiians") themselves were recruited as part of the HBC workforce as navigators and often settled anywhere it harboured in the Northwest and intermarrying with the local populations from present day [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia") all the way south to [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state) "Washington (state)") especially Fort Vancouver.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-74)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-75)

Extending the presence it had built in present-day British Columbia northern coast, the HBC reached by 1838 as far North as [Fort Stikine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Stikine "Fort Stikine") in the [Alaska Panhandle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Panhandle "Alaska Panhandle") by present-day [Wrangell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrangell "Wrangell"). The [RAC-HBC agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAC-HBC_agreement "RAC-HBC agreement") (1839) with the [Russian American Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_American_Company "Russian American Company") (RAC) provided for such a continuing presence in exchange for the HBC to supply the Russian coastal sites with agricultural products. The [Puget Sound Agricultural Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puget_Sound_Agricultural_Company "Puget Sound Agricultural Company") subsidiary was created to supply grain, dairy, livestock and manufactured goods out of Fort Vancouver, Fort Nisqually, [Fort Cowlitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowlitz_Farm "Cowlitz Farm") and [Fort Langley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Langley "Fort Langley") in present-day southern British Columbia.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-76)

The company's stranglehold on the region was broken by the [first successful large wagon train to reach Oregon in 1843](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Trail#Great_Migration_of_1843 "Oregon Trail"), led by [Marcus Whitman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Whitman "Marcus Whitman"). In the years that followed, thousands of emigrants poured into the [Willamette Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willamette_Valley "Willamette Valley") of Oregon. In 1846, the United States acquired full authority south of the [49th parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/49th_parallel_north "49th parallel north"); the most settled areas of the Oregon Country were south of the Columbia River in what is now Oregon. McLoughlin, who had once turned away would-be settlers when he was company director, then welcomed them from his general store at [Oregon City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_City,_Oregon "Oregon City, Oregon"). He later became known as the "Father of Oregon".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-77)

### Early presence in present-day Canada (British Columbia)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Early presence in present-day Canada (British Columbia)")]

The HBC also carried on the early presence in the region of the NWC in present-day central and northern [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia") with noteworthy sites: [Fort Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria,_British_Columbia "Alexandria, British Columbia"), [Fort d'Épinette (Fort St. John)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_St._John,_British_Columbia "Fort St. John, British Columbia"), [Fort St. James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_St._James "Fort St. James"), [Fort George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_George_(British_Columbia) "Prince George (British Columbia)") and [Fort Shuswap (Fort Kamloops)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamloops "Kamloops").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-78)

Since the 1818 Treaty settled the 49th parallel border only as far as the [Rocky Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains "Rocky Mountains"), the HBC was looking for a site further West in case the parallel border would become further extended at the end of the 10 years joint occupancy term. By 1824, the HBC was commissioning an expedition to travel from the [Fort George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Astoria "Fort Astoria") regional headquarter on the southern shore of the [Columbia River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_River "Columbia River") all the way to the [Fraser River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraser_River "Fraser River"). The three boats 40 some crew led by the [James McMillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_McMillan_(fur_trader) "James McMillan (fur trader)") were first to officially ever make it to [Puget Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puget_Sound "Puget Sound") from the continent, to reach its northern end into [Boundary Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundary_Bay "Boundary Bay") and to bypass the mouth of the Fraser. They shortcut through two mainland rivers and a portage in order to finally reach the lower Fraser. Friendly tribes were identified along with subsistence farming land suitable for sustaining a trading post. The first [Fort Langley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Langley_National_Historic_Site "Fort Langley National Historic Site") was subsequently built (1827), establishing an early settlers long lasting presence in current day southern British Columbia. The fur trade in a wet climate turned out to be marginal and quickly evolved into a salmon trade site with abundant supply in the vicinity.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-79)

The HBC stretched its presence North on the coastline with [Fort Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Simpson_(Columbia_Department) "Fort Simpson (Columbia Department)") (1831) on the [Nass River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nass_River "Nass River"), [Fort McLoughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_McLoughlin "Fort McLoughlin") (1833) and the [Beaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver_(steamship) "Beaver (steamship)") (1836), the first steamship to ever roam the Pacific Northwest for resupplying its coastline sites. The HBC was securing a trading monopoly on the coastline keeping away independent American traders: "By 1837, American competition on the North West Coast was effectively over".[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMackie1998126-80)

The HBC gained more control of the fur trade with both the coastline and inland tribes to access the fur rich [New Caledonia district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Caledonia_(Canada) "New Caledonia (Canada)") in current day northern British Columbia: "monopoly control of the coastal fur trade allowed the HBC to impose a uniform tariff on both sides of the Coast Mountains".[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMackie1998133-81)

By 1843, under pressure from the Americans to withdraw further North with the looming [Oregon Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Treaty "Oregon Treaty") border negotiation finalized in 1846, and strong of its coastal presence on the northern coast, HBC built [Fort Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Victoria_(British_Columbia) "Fort Victoria (British Columbia)") at the southern end of present-day [Vancouver Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver_Island "Vancouver Island") in southern BC. A well sheltered ocean port with agricultural potential in the vicinity would allow the new regional headquarter to further develop the trade on salmon, timber and cranberries. Trade via the Hawaiian post was also increasing. The [Fort Rupert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Rupert "Fort Rupert") (1849) at the northern end of the island would open up access to coal fields. On the continent mainland, [Fort Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope,_British_Columbia "Hope, British Columbia") and [Fort Yale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale,_British_Columbia "Yale, British Columbia") (1848) were built to extend the HBC presence on the [Fraser River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraser_River "Fraser River") as far as navigable. Brigades would link a rebuilt [Fort Langley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Langley "Fort Langley") (1840) on the Lower Fraser to [Fort Kamloops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamloops "Kamloops") by 1850 and the rest of the transportation network to [York Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Factory "York Factory") on the [Hudson Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay "Hudson Bay") along with the [New Caledonia district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Caledonia_(Canada) "New Caledonia (Canada)") fur returns.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-82)

### End of monopoly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: End of monopoly")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/A_Section_of_a_General_Map_of_the_Routes_in_British_North_America_Explored_by_the_Expedition_Under_Captain_Palliser_%281865%29_%282211818555%29.jpg/250px-A_Section_of_a_General_Map_of_the_Routes_in_British_North_America_Explored_by_the_Expedition_Under_Captain_Palliser_%281865%29_%282211818555%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_Section_of_a_General_Map_of_the_Routes_in_British_North_America_Explored_by_the_Expedition_Under_Captain_Palliser_(1865)_(2211818555).jpg)

A section of a map showing the routes explored during the [Palliser expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palliser_expedition "Palliser expedition")

The Guillaume Sayer trial in 1849 contributed to the end of the HBC monopoly. [Guillaume Sayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillaume_Sayer "Guillaume Sayer"), a [Métis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9tis_people_(Canada) "Métis people (Canada)") trapper and trader, was accused of illegal trading in furs. The Court of [Assiniboia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assiniboia "Assiniboia") brought Sayer to trial, before a jury of HBC officials and supporters. During the trial, a crowd of armed Métis men led by [Louis Riel Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Riel_Sr. "Louis Riel Sr.") gathered outside the courtroom. Although Sayer was found guilty of illegal trade, having evaded the HBC monopoly, Judge [Adam Thom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Thom "Adam Thom") did not levy a fine or punishment. Some accounts attributed that to the intimidating armed crowd gathered outside the courthouse. With the cry, "_Le commerce est libre! Le commerce est libre!_" ("Trade is free! Trade is free!"), the Métis loosened the HBC's previous control of the courts, which had enforced their monopoly on the settlers of Red River.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-83)

Another factor was the findings of the [Palliser Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palliser_Expedition "Palliser Expedition") of 1857 to 1860,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-84) led by Captain [John Palliser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Palliser "John Palliser").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-85) He surveyed the area of the prairies and wilderness from Lake Superior to the southern passes of the Rocky Mountains.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-86) Although he recommended against settlement of the region,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-87) the report sparked a debate. It fuelled the ongoing debate over the region's agricultural potential, challenging the position of the Hudson's Bay Company, which had long disputed that the Canadian West was capable of agricultural settlement.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-88)

In 1863, the [International Financial Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Financial_Society?action=edit&redlink=1 "International Financial Society (page does not exist)") bought controlling interest in the HBC, signalling a shift in the company's outlook: most of the new shareholders were less interested in the fur trade than in real estate speculation and economic development in the West. The Society floated £2 million in public shares on non-ceded land held ostensibly by the Hudson's Bay Company as an asset and leveraged this asset for collateral for these funds. These funds allowed the Society the financial means to weather the [financial collapse of 1866](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1866 "Panic of 1866"), which destroyed many competitors, and invest in railways in North America.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-89)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Canada_provinces_1867-1870.png/250px-Canada_provinces_1867-1870.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Canada_provinces_1867-1870.png)

Map of [British North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_North_America "British North America") in 1870, prior to HBC ceding [Rupert's Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupert's_Land "Rupert's Land") and the [North-Western Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North-Western_Territory "North-Western Territory") to Canada

In 1869, after rejecting the American government offer of CA$10 million,[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-90) the company approved the return of Rupert's Land to Britain. The government gave it to Canada and loaned the new country the £300,000 required to compensate HBC for its losses.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-H-2-91) HBC also received one-twentieth of the fertile areas to be opened for settlement and retained title to the lands on which it had built trading establishments.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-92) The deal, known as the [Deed of Surrender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deed_of_Surrender "Deed of Surrender"), came into force the following year. The resulting territory, the [North-West Territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North-West_Territories "North-West Territories"), was brought under Canadian jurisdiction under the terms of the [Rupert's Land Act 1868](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupert's_Land_Act_1868 "Rupert's Land Act 1868"), enacted by the Parliament of the United Kingdom. The Deed enabled the admission of the fifth province, [Manitoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoba "Manitoba"), to the [Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Confederation "Canadian Confederation") on 15 July 1870, the same day that the deed itself came into force.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-93)

During the 19th century the Hudson's Bay Company went through great changes in response to such factors as growth of population and new settlements in part of its territory, and ongoing pressure from Britain. It seemed unlikely that it would continue to control the future of the West.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-94)

### Shift to department stores

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Shift to department stores")]

See also: [Hudson's Bay (department store)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_(department_store) "Hudson's Bay (department store)")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Hudsons_Bay_Company_on_Cordova_Street.jpg/250px-Hudsons_Bay_Company_on_Cordova_Street.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hudsons_Bay_Company_on_Cordova_Street.jpg)

An [HBC store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_(department_store) "Hudson's Bay (department store)") in [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver"), c.1890s

The modern department store evolved from trading posts at the start of the 19th century, when they began to see demand for general merchandise grow rapidly. HBC soon expanded into the interior and set-up posts along river settlements that later developed into the modern cities of Winnipeg, [Calgary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgary "Calgary") and [Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton "Edmonton"). In 1857, the first sales shop was established in [Fort Langley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Langley "Fort Langley"). This was followed by other sales shops in [Fort Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria,_British_Columbia "Victoria, British Columbia") (1859), Winnipeg (1881), Calgary (1884), [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver") (1887), [Vernon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon,_British_Columbia "Vernon, British Columbia") (1887), Edmonton (1890), [Yorkton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkton "Yorkton") (1898), and [Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_British_Columbia "Nelson, British Columbia") (1902). The first of the grand "original six" department stores was built in Calgary in 1913. The other department stores that followed were in Edmonton, Vancouver, Victoria, [Saskatoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatoon "Saskatoon"), and Winnipeg.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-HH-3-95)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-96)

## 20th-century history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 20th-century history")]

The [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") interrupted a major remodelling and restoration of retail trade shops planned in 1912. Following the war, the company revitalized its fur trade and real estate activities, and diversified its operations by venturing into the oil business.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-HBC_Heritage-97)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-98) During the [Russian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Civil_War "Russian Civil War"), the company briefly operated in the [Siberian far east](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Far_East "Russian Far East"), even obtaining an agreement with the [Soviet government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_People's_Commissars_of_the_Russian_Soviet_Federative_Socialist_Republic "Council of People's Commissars of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic") until departing in 1924.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-99) The company co-founded [Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Oil_and_Gas_Company "Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company") (HBOG) in 1926 with [Marland Oil Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marland_Oil_Company "Marland Oil Company") (which merged with [Conoco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conoco "Conoco") in 1929). Although the company diversified into a number of areas, its department store business is the only remaining part of the company's operations, in the form of department stores under the Hudson's Bay brand.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Funding_Universe-100) The company also established new trading posts in the Canadian Arctic.

### Indigenous health

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Indigenous health")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Model_of_Hudson%27s_Bay_House%2C_Bishopsgate%2C_City_of_London.png/250px-Model_of_Hudson%27s_Bay_House%2C_Bishopsgate%2C_City_of_London.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Model_of_Hudson's_Bay_House,_Bishopsgate,_City_of_London.png)

Model of Hudson's Bay House at 52-68 Bishopsgate in London, designed in 1926 by [Mewès](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mew%C3%A8s "Charles Mewès")&[Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Joseph_Davis "Arthur Joseph Davis"). The building served as the company's headquarters until November 1940.

The medical scientist [Frederick Banting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Banting "Frederick Banting") was travelling in the Arctic in 1927 when he realized that crew or passengers on board the HBC paddle wheeler [_Distributor_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributor_(HBC_vessel) "Distributor (HBC vessel)") were responsible for spreading the influenza virus down the [Slave River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_River "Slave River") and [Mackenzie River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mackenzie_River "Mackenzie River"). Less than a decade after [the 1918 global flu pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_flu "Spanish flu"), a similar virus spread territory-wide over the summer and autumn, devastating the Indigenous population of the north.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Jackson-1965-101)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-102) Returning from the trip, Banting gave an interview in Montreal with a _[Toronto Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto\_Star "Toronto Star")_ reporter under the agreement that his statements on HBC would remain off the record.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Jackson-1965-101) The newspaper nonetheless published the conversation, which rapidly reached a wide audience across Europe and Australia.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Jackson-1965-101)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Tester-2008-103) Banting was angry at the leak, having promised the Department of the Interior not to make any statements to the press prior to clearing them.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Tester-2008-103)

The article noted that Banting had given the journalist C. R. Greenaway repeated instances of how the fox fur trade always favoured the company: "For over $100,000 of fox skins, he estimated that the Eskimos had not received $5,000 worth of goods."[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Tester-2008-103) He traced this treatment to health, consistent with reports made in previous years by RCMP officers, suggesting that "the result was a diet of 'flour, [sea-biscuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_tack "Hard tack"), tea and tobacco,' with the skins that once were used for clothing traded merely for 'cheap whiteman's goods.'"[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Tester-2008-103)

The HBC fur trade commissioner called Banting's remarks "false and slanderous", and a month later, the governor and general manager met Banting at the [King Edward Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Omni_King_Edward_Hotel "The Omni King Edward Hotel") to demand a retraction.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Jackson-1965-101)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Tester-2008-103) Banting stated that the reporter had betrayed his confidence, but did not retract his statement and reaffirmed that HBC was responsible for the death of Indigenous residents by supplying the wrong kind of food and introducing diseases into the Arctic.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Jackson-1965-101) As [A. Y. Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._Y._Jackson "A. Y. Jackson"), the [Group of Seven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_Seven_(artists) "Group of Seven (artists)") painter with whom Banting was travelling, noted in his memoir that since neither the governor nor the general manager had been to the Arctic, the meeting ended with them asking Banting's advice on what HBC ought to do: "He gave them some good advice and later he received a card at Christmas with the Governor's best wishes."[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Jackson-1965-101)

Banting maintained this position in his report to the Department of the Interior:[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Tester-2008-103)

> He noted that "infant mortality was high because of the undernourishment of the mother before birth"; that "white man's food leads to decay of native teeth"; that "tuberculosis has commenced. Saw several cases at Godhavn, Etah, Port Burwell, Arctic Bay"; that "an epidemic resembling influenza killed a considerable proportion of population at Port Burwell"; and that "the gravest danger faces the Eskimo in his transfer from a race-long hunter to a dependent trapper. White flour, sea-biscuits, tea and tobacco do not provide sufficient fuel to warm and nourish him". Furthermore, he discouraged the establishment of an Arctic hospital. The "proposed hospital at Pangnirtung would be a waste of money, as it could be reached by only a few natives". Banting's report contrasted starkly with the bland descriptions provided by the ship's physician, F. H. Stringer.

### Latter 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Latter 20th century")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Edificio_Henry_Morgan%2C_Montreal%2C_Canad%C3%A1%2C_2017-08-11%2C_DD_43.jpg/250px-Edificio_Henry_Morgan%2C_Montreal%2C_Canad%C3%A1%2C_2017-08-11%2C_DD_43.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edificio_Henry_Morgan,_Montreal,_Canad%C3%A1,_2017-08-11,_DD_43.jpg)

[Hudson's Bay Montreal Downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Montreal_Downtown "Hudson's Bay Montreal Downtown"). Originally the flagship store for [Morgan's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan's "Morgan's"), the department store chain was acquired by HBC in 1960.

HBOG also expanded during the 1960s, as it began shipping Canadian crude through a new link to the Glacier pipeline and on to the refinery in [Billings, Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billings,_Montana "Billings, Montana"). The company became the sixth-largest Canadian oil producer in 1967.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-104)

In 1970, on the company's 300th anniversary, as a result of punishing new British tax laws, the company relocated to Canada, and was rechartered as a Canadian business corporation under Canadian law,[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-105) Head Office functions were transferred from London to Winnipeg. By 1974, as the company expanded into eastern Canada, head office functions were moved to Toronto.

In 1972, the company acquired the four-store [Shop-Rite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shop-Rite_(Canada) "Shop-Rite (Canada)") chain of [catalogue stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalog_merchant "Catalog merchant"). The chain quickly expanded to 65 stores in Ontario, but closed in 1982 due to declining sales.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-106) In these stores, little merchandise was displayed; customers made their selections from catalogues, and staff would retrieve the merchandise from storerooms. The HBC also acquired [Freimans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freimans "Freimans") department stores in Ottawa and converted them to The Bay.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-107)

In 1973, HBOG acquired a 35 per cent stake in Siebens Oil and Gas, and, in 1979, it divested that interest. In 1980, it bought a controlling interest in Roxy Petroleum.

In 1978, the [Zellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zellers "Zellers") discount store chain made a bid to acquire the HBC; however, the HBC turned the tables and acquired Zellers.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-108)

In 1979, Canadian billionaire [Kenneth Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Thomson,_2nd_Baron_Thomson_of_Fleet "Kenneth Thomson, 2nd Baron Thomson of Fleet") won control of the company in a battle with [George Weston Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Weston_Limited "George Weston Limited"), and acquired a 75 per cent stake for $400 million.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-CanEncycl_HBC-109) Thomson sold the company's oil and gas business, financial services, distillery, and other interests for approximately $550 million, transforming the company into a leaner, more focused operation. In the 1980s, sales and oil prices slipped, while debt from acquisitions piled up which led to Hudson's Bay Company selling its 10.1 per cent stake in HBOG to [Dome Petroleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome_Petroleum "Dome Petroleum") in 1981.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-110) HBC lost $330 million from 1983 to 1988 and although it returned to profitability in the late 1980s, it was hit by the [early 1990s recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_1990s_recession "Early 1990s recession").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-111) On November 5, 1992, the Thomson family sold most of its stake in HBC but continued to be the largest shareholder.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-112) Thomson's remaining shares were ultimately sold five years later on September 15, 1997.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-113)

HBC sold its Canadian fur-auction business to Hudson's Bay Fur Sales Canada (now [North American Fur Auctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Fur_Auctions "North American Fur Auctions")). The Northern Stores Division was sold that same year to a group of investors and employees, which adopted [The North West Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_North_West_Company "The North West Company") name three years later.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-HBC.com_HBC_Heritage-114)

In 1991, the Bay agreed to stop retailing [fur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur "Fur") in response to complaints from people opposed to killing animals for this purpose.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-cbc.ca-115) In 1997, the Bay reopened its fur salons to meet consumer demand.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-cbc.ca-115)

## 21st-century history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 21st-century history")]

### 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 2000s")]

In December 2003, Maple Leaf Heritage Investments, a [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia")-based company created to acquire shares of Hudson's Bay Company, announced that it was considering making an offer to acquire all or some of the common shares of Hudson's Bay Company.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Privco-116) Maple Leaf Heritage Investments is a subsidiary of B-Bay Inc. Its CEO and chairman is American businesswoman [Anita Zucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Zucker "Anita Zucker"), widow of [Jerry Zucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Zucker_(businessman) "Jerry Zucker (businessman)"). Zucker had previously been the head of the Polymer Group, which acquired another Canadian institution, [Dominion Textile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_Textile "Dominion Textile").

It had been a member of the [International Association of Department Stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Association_of_Department_Stores "International Association of Department Stores") from 2001 to 2005.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-117) On 26 January 2006, the HBC's board agreed to a bid from Jerry Zucker. The [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina") based billionaire financier was a longtime HBC minority shareholder. In a 9 March 2006 press release,[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-118) the HBC announced that Zucker would replace [Yves Fortier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Fortier_(lawyer) "Yves Fortier (lawyer)") as governor and [George Heller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Heller "George Heller") as CEO, becoming the first US citizen to lead the company. After Jerry Zucker's death in April 2008 from [brain cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain_cancer "Brain cancer"), the board named his widow, Anita Zucker, as HBC Governor and HBC Deputy-Governor Rob Johnston as CEO.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Privco-116)

From 2004 to 2008, the HBC owned and operated a small chain of off-price stores called [Designer Depot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Designer_Depot "Designer Depot"). The concept was similar to the [Winners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winners "Winners") and [HomeSense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HomeSense "HomeSense") retail format, but Designer Depot did not meet sales expectations, and its nine stores were sold.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-119)

On 16 July 2008 shortly after Zucker’s death, the company was sold to [NRDC Equity Partners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRDC_Equity_Partners "NRDC Equity Partners") for just over $1.1 billion,[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-120) a private equity firm based in [Purchase, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchase,_New_York "Purchase, New York"), which already owned [Lord & Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_&_Taylor "Lord & Taylor"), the oldest department store in the United States.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-GT-DEX-2008-19-121)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-122) The Canadian and US holdings were transferred to NRDC Equity Partners' holding company, [Hudson's Bay Trading Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Trading_Company "Hudson's Bay Trading Company"), as of late 2008.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-123)

### 2010s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 2010s")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/d5/Hudson%27s_Bay_Company_%28emblem%29.svg/250px-Hudson%27s_Bay_Company_%28emblem%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HBC_Logo.svg)

HBC's [coat of arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_the_Hudson's_Bay_Company "Coat of arms of the Hudson's Bay Company") logo (used from 2009 to 2013)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-Coat_of_Arms-124)

Another HBC chain, [Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fields_(department_store) "Fields (department store)"), was sold to a private firm in 2012.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-125) Established in 1950, Fields was acquired by [Zellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zellers "Zellers") in 1976. When Zellers was acquired by HBC in 1978, Fields became part of the HBC portfolio.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-126)

In October 2012, the HBC announced a $1.6-billion [initial public offering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") (IPO); Baker planned to use the IPO to allow Canadian ownership to return to the company, and to help pay off debts with other partners.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-127)

In January 2016, HBC announced it would expand deeper into digital space with the acquisition of an [online](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce") flash sales site, the [Gilt Groupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilt_Groupe "Gilt Groupe"), for [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")250,000,000.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-128)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-129) HBC also announced its expansion into the Netherlands in May 2016 with the takeover of 20 former [Vroom & Dreesmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vroom_&_Dreesmann "Vroom & Dreesmann") (V&D) sites by 2017. V&D, a historic Dutch department store chain, had gone [bankrupt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankrupt "Bankrupt") and shut down in early 2016.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-130) As of November 2017, the company also expanded retail operations into Europe, including five Saks Off Fifth stores in Germany.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-financialpost.com-131)

In early 2017, the Hudson's Bay Company made an overture to [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's") for a potential takeover of the US department store chain. Later, HBC also considered a purchase of [Neiman Marcus Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neiman_Marcus_Group "Neiman Marcus Group") Inc. It did not proceed with either deal.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-132)

On 1 April 2018, HBC disclosed that more than five million credit and debit cards used for in-store purchases had been recently breached by hackers. The compromised credit card transactions took place at Saks Fifth Avenue, Saks Off 5th, and Lord & Taylor stores. The hack had been discovered by Gemini Advisory, which called the breach "amongst the biggest and most damaging to ever hit retail companies".[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-133) A July 2019 hack of [Capital One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_One "Capital One"), which provides HBC Mastercards, did not affect the HBC credit cards or card applications, according to HBC.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-134)

In June 2019, a consortium including chairman [Richard Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_A._Baker_(businessman) "Richard A. Baker (businessman)"), [Rhône Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rh%C3%B4ne_Group "Rhône Group"), [WeWork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WeWork "WeWork"), Hanover Investments ([Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxembourg "Luxembourg")) and Abrams Capital Management announced that it wanted to take the company private.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-135) The group then owned just over 50 per cent of HBC shares. In mid-August, the consortium said that it owned 57 per cent of the HBC shares. By 19 August 2019, however, Canadian investment firm [Catalyst Capital Group Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton_Glassman "Newton Glassman") said it had acquired enough shares to block the plan. A US company, Land & Buildings Investment Management, the owner of over 6 per cent of the shares, had also criticized the Baker plan.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-136)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-137)[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-138) In March 2020, Baker and a group of shareholders were successful in taking the company private.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-139)

HBC sold [Galeria Kaufhof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galeria_Kaufhof "Galeria Kaufhof"), [Galeria Inno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galeria_Inno "Galeria Inno"), [Gilt Groupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilt_Groupe "Gilt Groupe"), and [Lord & Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_&_Taylor "Lord & Taylor") by August 2019. A feature article by [Bloomberg News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_News "Bloomberg News") mentioned that CEO [Helena Foulkes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helena_Foulkes "Helena Foulkes"), recruited in 2018, "had helped improve the bottom line at Hudson's Bay". She was selling assets "to put the company on more solid financial footing" and could then focus on Saks Fifth Avenue and the Bay. On the other hand, Bloomberg suggested that millennial shoppers prefer to make purchases online, or direct from various brands' own stores, and that HBC "has yet to offer something they can't find somewhere else and risks drifting into irrelevance".[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-140)

### 2020s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hudson%27s_Bay_Company&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: 2020s")]

In February 2020, shareholders of the company voted in favour of a plan to become a private company at a special meeting of shareholders. Under the plan of arrangement, the company was to be owned by a group of continuing shareholders led by HBC governor and executive chairman Richard Baker. Effective 3 March 2020, the company was delisted from the [Toronto Stock Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Stock_Exchange "Toronto Stock Exchange"), with [Richard A. Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_A._Baker_(businessman) "Richard A. On March 16, 2022, it was announced that HBC and [Sycamore Partners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sycamore_Partners "Sycamore Partners") were preparing bids to buy [Kohl's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kohl's "Kohl's").[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-143)

In 2023, Hudson's Bay officially stopped selling animal fur products.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson's_Bay_Company#cite_note-144)
